description: Long-stay, remote-work and nomad visa records, one per country, each sourced to an official government page and carrying the date it was last checked.
null_means: null means the government has not published this rule. It never means "no".

records.summary: Albania is one of Europe's cheapest and most underrated nomad bases — Adriatic and Ionian beaches, a fast-growing scene in Tirana, and a remarkably low cost of living. Its digital nomad route (a Type D visa plus a Unique Permit for 'digital mobile workers') has one of the lowest income bars on the continent, around $815/month, and can be renewed annually for up to five years. The application is fully online.
requirements: Remote income of at least about $9,800/year (~$815/month), from companies or clients outside Albania
Remote work for a foreign employer, freelancing for international clients, or a business registered abroad
Income earned exclusively from non-Albanian sources
Valid passport
Health insurance valid in Albania
Proof of accommodation or address in Albania
steps: Confirm your income meets the ~$815/month threshold from foreign sources
Create an account on Albania's official e-visa portal (e-visa.al)
Select the Type D long-stay visa and the 'digital mobile worker' option, and complete the form
Upload documents (passport, proof of remote income, insurance, address) and pay the ~€120 fee
On approval, enter Albania and obtain the Unique Permit; renew annually for up to five years total

faqs.question: Does Albania have an official digital nomad visa?
faqs.answer: Not under that exact name. Albania's nomad route combines a Type D long-stay visa with a Unique Permit for 'digital mobile workers,' introduced in 2022. In practice it functions as a digital nomad visa and is applied for entirely online.

faqs.question: How long can I stay in Albania?
faqs.answer: The permit is issued for one year and can be renewed annually for up to five years total — one of the longer runways among nomad visas, paired with one of the lowest income requirements.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Albania?
faqs.answer: If you spend more than 183 days in Albania you may become a tax resident. Albania has relatively low tax rates, but treatment of foreign income depends on your situation — confirm with a local accountant before a long stay.

faqs.question: How cheap is Albania really?
faqs.answer: It's among the most affordable countries in Europe — rent, food, and daily costs run well below Western Europe, which combined with the ~$815/month income bar makes it one of the most accessible nomad bases on the continent.

records.renewal_note: One year to start, then renewals that lengthen — two years, then five — and after five continuous years you can apply for permanent residence, with naturalisation possible at seven. Permanent residence isn't automatic at the five-year mark: Albania also asks for Albanian language ability, evidence of integration and stable finances.
records.tax_note: We could not find a published nomad-specific tax exemption here, and we are not going to assume one exists — nor assume it doesn't. What is solid: residents are taxed on worldwide income, and passing 183 days in a year normally makes you resident. Confirm the current position with the national tax authority before you plan around it.

records.summary: Antigua and Barbuda offers 365 beaches and a relaxed Caribbean pace under one of the region's longer nomad visas — two full years. You'll need $50,000/year in income and a $1,500 fee, but there's no local income tax and approval is fast. A strong pick for a longer Caribbean stay, family included.
requirements: Expected income of at least $50,000/year for each of the two years, earned outside Antigua and Barbuda
Remote work for an employer, clients, or business based abroad
Valid passport
Medical insurance covering the intended stay
Police clearance for each applicant over 16
steps: Confirm you can show at least $50,000/year in foreign income
Gather documents: passport, proof of income, medical insurance, police clearance
Apply online through the official Nomad Digital Residence portal
Pay the $1,500 fee (single; family fees apply, plus $650 per dependent beyond three)
Receive approval (typically 5–7 working days); the visa allows up to two years

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: Up to two years — one of the longer Caribbean nomad visas — and your immediate family can join you.

faqs.question: Will I pay income tax?
faqs.answer: No. Nomad Digital Residence holders and their dependents don't pay local income tax during their stay.

faqs.question: What's the income requirement?
faqs.answer: At least $50,000/year for each of the two years of the visa, earned from outside Antigua and Barbuda.

faqs.question: How fast is approval?
faqs.answer: Quick — typically 5 to 7 working days after a complete application.

records.renewal_note: The Nomad Digital Residence runs two years, and sources genuinely disagree on whether it can be renewed at all — some state it is issued once and cannot be extended, others describe a single renewal. Assume two years and no more unless the NDR programme office confirms otherwise. Either way it does not lead to residency: Antigua's settlement routes are separate, and the country's citizenship-by-investment programme is a different thing entirely.
records.tax_note: Antigua and Barbuda abolished personal income tax outright in 2016 — no tax on local or worldwide income, no capital gains, inheritance or wealth tax. As with the other zero-tax Caribbean jurisdictions, there is no special nomad regime because there is nothing to exempt you from.
records.family_note: The Nomad Digital Residence is explicitly designed to admit your immediate family alongside you for the two-year term.
records.logistics_note: Filed online through the government's dedicated Nomad Digital Residence portal — no consulate visit required.

records.summary: Argentina gives remote workers a low-friction way to live in Buenos Aires and beyond — European-feeling cities, a strong café and food culture, and a cost of living that swings in your favour. There's no fixed income minimum: you show stable foreign earnings via a simple migration process you can do yourself. The trade-off is a shorter horizon than most — 180 days, extendable once to a year.
requirements: Be a national of a country that can enter Argentina visa-free as a tourist — the visa is only open to those nationalities
Proof of stable, regular remote income from clients or companies based abroad (no fixed legal minimum; ~$1,500+/month is commonly shown)
A signed application describing your independent remote work
A short CV showing your experience and education level
Contracts, company endorsements, or income receipts with at least one occupational reference
Valid passport and international health insurance
Criminal background check (apostilled or legalised; translated to Spanish if needed)
steps: Confirm your nationality can enter Argentina visa-free — eligibility for this visa depends on it
Gather proof of remote work and income: contracts, invoices, or receipts, plus a CV and reference
Apostille or legalise foreign documents and translate them to Spanish where required
Apply through the Dirección Nacional de Migraciones (the process is personal and doesn't need an agent), or at an Argentine consulate
Receive a 180-day transitory residency, extendable once for another 180 days — up to a year total

faqs.question: Is there a minimum income for the Argentina nomad visa?
faqs.answer: There's no fixed legal minimum stated by Argentina's migration authority — you must demonstrate regular, stable income from foreign sources through contracts, invoices, or bank statements. In practice most applicants show around $1,500/month or more to satisfy the 'sufficient means' test.

faqs.question: Who is eligible to apply?
faqs.answer: The visa is only open to nationals of countries that don't need a visa for tourist entry to Argentina (which covers the US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia and many others). If your passport requires a tourist visa for Argentina, you can't use this route.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: The visa grants 180 days of transitory residency, which can be extended once for another 180 days — up to one year in total. After that you'd need to pursue a different residency category to stay longer.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Argentina?
faqs.answer: Short stays generally don't trigger Argentine tax on foreign income, and foreign-sourced income is often treated favourably for newcomers. Tax residency and treatment depend on your time in-country and situation — confirm with a local accountant if you plan to stay long.

records.renewal_note: 180 days as a residente transitorio, extendable once by 180 more — one year maximum. The extension expects you to have spent at least half the initial period in Argentina. Transitory residence counts toward neither permanent residency nor citizenship, which matters here because Argentine naturalisation is otherwise famously quick at two years — but you need a residency category that actually accrues, such as the Rentista.
records.tax_note: Stay under twelve months and foreign-sourced income is not taxed in Argentina — which lines up neatly with the visa's own one-year ceiling. Go beyond it and you trigger tax residency and worldwide taxation at progressive rates of 5–35%. There is no nomad-specific regime; the favourable treatment comes from simply not becoming resident.
records.logistics_note: Filed online, and unusually there is no officially published minimum income — in practice applicants are expected to show somewhere around $2,000–2,500 a month. Treat any specific figure you read as convention rather than rule.

records.summary: The Bahamas' BEATS program puts you on 700 islands of turquoise water within a short hop of the US east coast. There's no fixed income minimum — just proof you can support yourself — and approval is quick. The catch is cost: the Bahamas is expensive, with nomads typically spending several thousand a month. Renewable up to three years.
requirements: Proof of sufficient funds to support yourself and any dependents (no fixed income minimum) — typically 3–6 months of bank statements
Remote work for an employer, clients, or business outside the Bahamas
Valid passport with at least six months' validity
Medical insurance valid across the Bahamas for the stay
steps: Gather documents: passport, bank statements, proof of remote work, medical insurance
Apply online and pay the non-refundable $25 application fee
On approval, pay the permit fee — $1,000 for professionals ($500 for students), plus $500 per dependent
Receive approval (typically about 5 business days)
Travel to the Bahamas; the permit lasts one year and is renewable up to three years total

faqs.question: Is there an income requirement?
faqs.answer: No fixed minimum. You demonstrate sufficient funds via bank statements rather than meeting a set salary. Given the high cost of living, plan for several thousand a month regardless.

faqs.question: What does BEATS cost?
faqs.answer: A $25 application fee, then a $1,000 permit fee for professionals ($500 for students), plus $500 per dependent.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: One year, with annual renewals considered up to a maximum three-year stay.

faqs.question: Will I pay Bahamian tax?
faqs.answer: The Bahamas has no personal income tax, so your foreign earnings aren't taxed locally — though you may still owe tax in your home country.

records.renewal_note: One year, renewable twice — three years maximum. BEATS is explicitly a non-immigrant permit, so none of that time counts toward Bahamian permanent residence, which runs on its own economic and long-residence routes.
records.tax_note: The Bahamas has no personal income tax at all — none on wages, pensions, dividends or capital gains — so there is no nomad-specific concession because none is needed. Government revenue comes from VAT, duties and property taxes instead, which is worth factoring into cost of living. Your home country still taxes you on its own rules.

records.summary: Barbados led the Caribbean nomad-visa wave with its Welcome Stamp — a full year on a famously friendly, English-speaking island of pink-sand beaches and solid infrastructure. The income bar is high ($50,000/year) and the fee steep ($2,000), but there's no local income tax and approval is fast. Best for established earners wanting Caribbean island life.
requirements: Expected income of at least $50,000/year, earned outside Barbados
Remote work for an employer, clients, or business based outside Barbados
Valid passport
Valid health insurance for the duration of your stay
Application fee of $2,000 (individual) or $3,000 (family)
steps: Confirm you expect to earn at least $50,000 over the next 12 months from outside Barbados
Gather documents: passport, proof of income, health insurance
Apply online for the Welcome Stamp
Pay the $2,000 individual fee ($3,000 for families) on approval
Receive approval (typically about 7 business days) and travel; the stamp is valid 12 months

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Barbados on the Welcome Stamp?
faqs.answer: No. Welcome Stamp holders don't pay Barbadian income tax on their foreign earnings — a key draw despite the high fee.

faqs.question: How much does it cost?
faqs.answer: $2,000 for an individual or $3,000 for a family, and you must show $50,000/year in income. Renewals get a 25% discount on the fee.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: Up to 12 months from approval, with no minimum-stay obligation, and it can be renewed.

faqs.question: Is the program still running?
faqs.answer: Yes — as of 2026 the Welcome Stamp is confirmed to continue at least through the end of 2026. Check the official site for the latest status before applying.

records.renewal_note: Twelve months, renewable annually. The Welcome Stamp is a visitor-class permission and does not itself grant residency; Barbados has a separate five-year route to permanent residence for people residing as immigrants, which this stamp does not put you on. Check the programme still exists before planning: Cabinet has approved it only through 31 December 2026.
records.tax_note: Unusually explicit, and in your favour: Welcome Stamp holders are deemed NOT tax resident in Barbados and pay no Barbadian income tax on foreign earnings — and that holds even if you spend more than 182 days in the country during the tax year, which is normally the exact line that catches people. The programme's own end date (currently 31 December 2026) is the thing to watch, not the tax treatment.

records.summary: Brazil's VITEM XIV opens one of South America's biggest, most varied countries to remote workers — beaches, big cities, and a low cost of living outside the hotspots — at a modest $1,500/month income bar. The catch is paperwork: every foreign document must be apostilled, and that's the single most common reason applications stall. The visa is valid for one year and renewable for a second.
requirements: Proof of remote foreign income of at least $1,500/month, or available bank savings of at least $18,000
A work or service contract showing you're employed by or contracting for a company outside Brazil
Valid passport with sufficient remaining validity
Apostilled criminal background check — the most common rejection point when missing or incorrect
Health insurance valid in Brazil
Proof you work over the internet and not for a Brazilian employer
Completed application forms and passport photos
steps: Confirm you meet the $1,500/month income (or $18,000 savings) test
Apostille your documents under the Hague Convention — the criminal record especially; missing apostilles are the top rejection reason
Gather income proof (often six months of bank statements or a tax return), contracts, insurance, and passport
Apply at a Brazilian consulate abroad, or online via MigranteWeb if you're already inside Brazil
Receive the one-year visa (renewable for a second year) in roughly 15–30 business days

faqs.question: Do I really need to apostille my documents?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's the single most important step. Every foreign-issued document — especially your criminal background check — must be apostilled under the Hague Convention. Missing or incorrect apostilles are the most common reason Brazilian nomad visa applications are rejected.

faqs.question: Can I apply from inside Brazil?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you're already in Brazil you can apply online through the MigranteWeb system; from abroad you apply at a Brazilian consulate. Processing from inside Brazil typically runs 15–30 business days.

faqs.question: How is my income taxed in Brazil?
faqs.answer: If you spend more than 183 days in Brazil within a 12-month period you generally become a tax resident and may owe Brazilian tax on worldwide income; below that you usually don't. Brazil's tax rules are complex — confirm your situation with a local accountant before a long stay.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: The visa is valid for one year and can be renewed once for a second year, for two years total. After that you'd need to look at other Brazilian residency routes.

records.renewal_note: Resolution 45/2021 gives one year plus one renewal — two years is what you are entitled to. Third years have been granted in practice through 2026, but treat that as discretion rather than a rule you can plan around. No number of renewals turns into permanent residency: people who stay switch lanes entirely (marriage or união estável, retirement income, investment, work). File through MigranteWeb before the current residence expires, or it becomes a fresh application.
records.tax_note: Brazil is stricter than most and catches people out: cumulative presence above 183 days in any rolling 12-month window triggers automatic fiscal residency — a rolling window, not a calendar year, and regardless of which visa you hold. Once resident you are taxed on worldwide income at progressive rates up to 27.5%. There is no digital-nomad exemption.
records.family_note: Dependants add roughly $500/month each to the income requirement. Expect apostilled and sworn-translated proof of the relationship for each one, plus their own passport and background check — the translation step is the slow part, so start it early.
records.logistics_note: Either at a Brazilian consulate before travelling or in-country. Renewals go through MigranteWeb and must be filed before the current residence expires — miss the window and it is treated as a fresh application rather than an extension.

records.summary: Cape Verde is an Atlantic island chain off West Africa — year-round warmth, beaches, and a relaxed Creole-Portuguese culture, in a timezone friendly to both Europe and the Americas. Its Remote Working Program is cheap and fully online, and unusually it asks for an average bank balance rather than a fixed salary. You get six months, renewable.
requirements: An average bank balance of at least €1,500 over the last six months (€2,700 for families) — balance-based, not a fixed salary
Remote work as a freelancer or employee for clients or a company outside Cape Verde
Valid passport with at least six months' validity
Proof of health insurance
Accommodation booking in Cape Verde
Criminal background check
Eligible nationality (Europe, North America, Portuguese-speaking/CPLP, or ECOWAS countries)
steps: Confirm your six-month average bank balance meets the €1,500 (individual) or €2,700 (family) requirement
Gather documents: passport, six months of bank statements, insurance, accommodation booking, criminal record
Apply online through Cape Verde's Remote Working portal and pay the ~€20 application fee
Get approval (usually about two to four weeks) by email
Travel to Cape Verde, pay the ~€34 airport security tax on entry, and collect your six-month residence permit

faqs.question: Is the requirement income or savings?
faqs.answer: Savings/balance, not salary. Cape Verde asks for an average bank balance of about €1,500 over the previous six months for individuals (€2,700 for families) — a different test from the monthly-income requirements most countries use.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: The permit is valid for six months and can be renewed. After renewals some nomads extend further or move to longer residency, but the base grant is half a year.

faqs.question: Who is eligible to apply?
faqs.answer: The program is open to remote workers from Europe, North America, Portuguese-speaking (CPLP) countries, and ECOWAS (West African) states. Check your nationality qualifies before applying.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Cape Verde?
faqs.answer: Short stays on the remote working program generally don't trigger local income tax on foreign earnings. Confirm your specific situation if you renew and stay long-term.

records.renewal_note: Six months, renewable once for another six — a year in total. It is issued as a combined temporary work and tourism visa rather than a residence permit, so treat settlement as an entirely separate application.
records.tax_note: We could not find a published position on how Cabo Verde treats digital nomad visa holders' foreign income, and we are not going to guess on a tax question. Confirm with the Direção Nacional de Receitas do Estado before you rely on any figure you read elsewhere.
records.family_note: Families are catered for with a separate threshold: about €1,500/month for an individual against roughly €2,700/month for a family, rather than a per-person add-on.

records.summary: The Cayman Islands ran one of the pandemic era's most exclusive nomad programs — the Global Citizen Concierge Program, a two-year stay for remote workers earning US$100,000+ — and then quietly closed it. As of 2026 it is not accepting applications, making Cayman one of several island programs (Bermuda's went the same way) to shut once tourism recovered. Remote workers can still visit on standard visitor entry; there is simply no dedicated nomad route anymore.
requirements: Status check (verified July 2026): the Global Citizen Concierge Program is closed — no new applications are being accepted
For reference, the closed program required proof of US$100,000+ annual salary (US$150,000 with a dependent), remote employment outside Cayman, health insurance, and an annual fee of roughly US$1,469
What you need today: standard visitor entry — many nationalities (US, UK, EU, Canada) visit without a pre-arranged visa, typically admitted for up to 30 days and extendable
Working for a Cayman employer or serving the local market requires a work permit through an employer — visitor status doesn't allow it
steps: Accept the honest premise: there is currently no nomad visa to apply for in the Cayman Islands
Short remote-work stints: enter as a visitor (most Western passports need no advance visa), keep your work fully remote for foreign employers, and extend locally if needed
Longer stays: the remaining routes are employment-based work permits or substantial-investment residence options — both categorically different from a nomad visa
Watch the official government channels for any relaunch; program pages from 2020–2023 still circulate and read as if the GCCP were open — check the date on anything you read

faqs.question: Is the Cayman Islands digital nomad visa still available?
faqs.answer: No. The Global Citizen Concierge Program stopped accepting applications and is closed as of 2026. It was among the first high-profile nomad programs to shut down — launched in late 2020 to offset collapsed tourism, wound down once visitors returned. Plenty of guides online still describe it in the present tense; they're out of date.

faqs.question: What did the program offer while it ran?
faqs.answer: A two-year residential certificate for remote workers and their families — at a price. Applicants needed a salary of at least US$100,000 (US$150,000 with one dependent, US$168,000 with two), proof of remote employment outside Cayman, insurance, and an annual fee of roughly US$1,469 plus card processing charges. It was deliberately aimed at high earners, in keeping with Cayman's tourism positioning.

faqs.question: Can I still work remotely from the Cayman Islands?
faqs.answer: As a visitor, briefly and informally — many nationalities enter without a pre-arranged visa for stays typically granted at up to 30 days, extendable through immigration. Answering emails for your foreign employer on a visit isn't policed, but there is no legal long-stay remote-work status anymore, and Cayman's cost of living is among the highest in the Caribbean. For a legal long stay, the realistic routes are an employer work permit or investment-based residence.

faqs.question: Which islands still have open nomad programs?
faqs.answer: The Caribbean landscape has thinned — Cayman and Bermuda both closed their programs — but options remain: Barbados, Antigua and Barbuda, Curacao, and the Bahamas have all operated remote-worker stays, and we track each one on its own country page. Programs in this region open and close with tourism cycles, so verify status on the official site before building plans around any of them.

records.summary: Colombia's nomad visa has the lowest income requirement of any major program — around three times the local minimum wage, roughly $1,400/month — for up to two years in Medellín's eternal spring, Bogotá's altitude, or the Caribbean coast. The application is online and decided in weeks.
requirements: Remote work for foreign companies/clients, or a digital-entrepreneurship project, fully online application
Monthly income of at least 3× the Colombian minimum wage (about $1,400 in 2026 — COP 5,252,715, resets each January with the minimum wage)
Bank statements for the last 3 months proving the income
Health insurance covering Colombia for the visa period
Letter describing your remote work or employer letter
steps: Prepare bank statements, work letter, insurance, passport scan, photo
Apply online via the Cancillería visa portal and pay the study fee
Respond to any document requests; on approval pay the visa fee
Receive the e-visa, enter Colombia, and register your visa (cédula de extranjería) if staying over 6 months

faqs.question: Do I become a Colombian tax resident on the nomad visa?
faqs.answer: If you stay 183+ days in any 365-day window, yes — and Colombia taxes worldwide income at meaningful rates. Many nomads deliberately keep stays under the threshold; if you'll exceed it, price the tax cost first.

faqs.question: Is the visa valid for multiple entries?
faqs.answer: Yes — it's multi-entry for its full validity (up to two years), so you can base yourself in Colombia and travel the region freely.

faqs.question: Is $1,400/month really enough to qualify and live there?
faqs.answer: To qualify, yes — it's the floor, pegged to local wages. To live well in Medellín or Bogotá you'll want more like $1,800–2,500/month; the visa's low bar just means almost any working nomad clears it.

records.renewal_note: Valid up to two years and renewable, but the V visa is a visitor category: none of that time counts toward Colombian residency. Only M-type visas (marriage, pension, investor, work) accumulate against the five years residency needs, so if settling is the plan you want to move onto an M as early as you can rather than stacking nomad renewals.
records.tax_note: Over 183 days in any 365-day period makes you a Colombian tax resident, taxed on worldwide income at progressive rates. There is no nomad exemption, which is why many people on the V visa deliberately stay under the line — four or five months, then a real break. Colombia does have double-taxation treaties (Spain, Canada, Chile, Mexico, Portugal, Czechia, South Korea and others) that prevent genuine double taxation for residents of those countries.
records.logistics_note: Filed online through the Cancillería. On the income bar, note that our USD figure and the ones circulating elsewhere don't agree: the requirement is legally pegged to 3× the Colombian minimum wage, and published conversions for 2026 range from roughly $750 to $1,400 a month depending on which wage figure and exchange rate is used. Work from the SMMLV multiple, not from anyone's dollar conversion.

records.summary: Costa Rica wrote its nomad visa into law with real perks: foreign income is tax-exempt, your home driver's license stays valid, and your work equipment enters duty-free. Pura vida plus surf, jungle, and one of the most stable democracies in the Americas — for a $3,000/month income bar.
requirements: Stable foreign income of at least $3,000/month (or $4,000/month covering family) over the last year, bank-documented
Remote work or services exclusively for employers/clients outside Costa Rica
Medical insurance covering the full stay in Costa Rica
Apostilled supporting documents; application via Migración
First permit covers 12 months, renewable once for 12 more if you spent at least 80 days in-country
steps: Compile 12 months of bank statements proving the income floor, apostilled and translated where required
Submit the application online or at Migración (or a consulate) with insurance and passport documents
Wait out processing, then complete registration and biometrics in Costa Rica
Renew at month 12 if you've met the minimum-presence requirement

faqs.question: Do digital nomads pay Costa Rican taxes?
faqs.answer: No — the law explicitly exempts your foreign-source remote income from Costa Rican income tax, and it also waives import duties on your work gear (laptops, cameras, equipment). It's one of the most concrete tax carve-outs of any nomad visa.

faqs.question: Is $3,000/month income enough to live in Costa Rica?
faqs.answer: Comfortably in most of the country, tightly in premium beach towns like Tamarindo or Santa Teresa during high season. San José suburbs and smaller coastal towns stretch the budget much further.

faqs.question: Can I just do border runs instead?
faqs.answer: Many do — tourist entries are typically 180 days now. But the nomad visa removes the gamble at the border, adds the tax exemption and license validity, and signals legal residence to banks and landlords.

records.renewal_note: One year, renewable once — and the renewal has teeth: you must have been physically in Costa Rica at least 180 days during that first year. It is a non-resident stay category, so none of it converts to residency. After two years you either leave or apply under Rentista, Pensionado or an investor category, each of which does lead to permanent residency after three years.
records.tax_note: Costa Rica taxes territorially, so income earned from foreign clients or employers is outside the Costa Rican income tax net, and the Estancia is written as a non-resident stay category. The trade-off is that this arrangement builds nothing: the routes that do lead to residency (Rentista, Pensionado, investor) come with their own tax posture.
records.family_note: The Estancia lets the main applicant sponsor accompanying family members. The income threshold is higher for a family than for a single applicant, so check which figure you are being quoted.

records.summary: Croatia was one of Europe's first movers on nomad visas, and the package is solid: up to 18 months of Adriatic coastline, no tax on your foreign remote income while on the permit, and an application you can start online. The catch — it doesn't renew, so it suits a long stay rather than a settling plan.
requirements: Remote work for a company or clients outside Croatia (or your own foreign-registered company)
Monthly income of 2.5× the average Croatian net salary — €3,622.50 in 2026 — or equivalent savings (~€65,205 for 18 months)
Proof of accommodation in Croatia and health insurance covering the whole stay
Clean criminal record certificate from your home country
Croatia is in Schengen — time on the permit doesn't consume your 90-day tourist allowance elsewhere
steps: Gather documents: work contracts, income statements or bank balance, insurance, accommodation proof, criminal record
Apply online via the Ministry of Interior portal, at a Croatian embassy, or at a police station if already in Croatia
Wait for approval, then register your address and biometrics at the local police station
Collect your residence card — valid up to 18 months, non-renewable (a fresh application needs 6 months outside Croatia)

faqs.question: Do digital nomads pay Croatian income tax?
faqs.answer: No — income from your foreign remote work is explicitly exempt from Croatian income tax while you hold the digital nomad permit. That makes Croatia one of the cleanest tax setups in Europe for a year-plus stay. Other obligations (like home-country taxes) still apply.

faqs.question: Can I renew the Croatian nomad permit?
faqs.answer: Not back-to-back. When the permit expires you must spend six months outside Croatia before applying again. If you want a long-term European base, look at Portugal or Spain instead.

faqs.question: Can my family join me in Croatia?
faqs.answer: Yes — close family members can apply for temporary stay at the same time, with the income requirement increased by roughly 10% per family member.

records.renewal_note: Issued for up to 18 months and deliberately not renewable back-to-back: you must leave Croatia for at least six months before applying again. Time on this permit counts toward neither permanent residency nor naturalisation. It's a long stay, not a move.
records.tax_note: Croatia's is one of the cleanest arrangements in Europe: holders of the digital nomad permit are exempt from Croatian income tax on foreign-sourced income, and unusually that exemption holds even past the 183-day mark that would normally make you tax resident. The catch is the permit itself — 18 months, non-renewable — so the tax benefit has a hard expiry. Your home country still taxes you on its own terms.
records.family_note: A partner and children can join, with the income threshold rising roughly 10–20% per additional family member. Read the fine print on work rights though: an accompanying spouse cannot simply take a Croatian job on the strength of your permit.
records.logistics_note: Can be filed at a Croatian consulate before travelling or at a local police administration once in Croatia. Note the income figure moved for 2026 — older guides quote roughly €3,295.

records.summary: Curaçao blends Dutch-Caribbean culture, colorful Willemstad, and reliably sunny weather on the edge of the hurricane belt. Its @HOME program is fully online, moderately priced, and asks for around €2,600/month — and foreign income isn't taxed locally. You get six months, renewable once for a year total.
requirements: Verifiable income of at least about €2,600/month (≈$2,800), from outside Curaçao
Ability to work independently online — for a foreign employer, a foreign company you co-own, or foreign freelance clients
Valid passport
Health insurance
Proof of accommodation and a return flight ticket
Clean criminal record
steps: Confirm your income meets the ~€2,600/month threshold from foreign sources
Gather documents (English, Dutch, or Spanish accepted): passport, proof of income, insurance, accommodation, return ticket, criminal record
Apply online through the @HOME in Curaçao portal
Pay the application fee of about ANG 535 (~$300)
On approval, travel to Curaçao; the permit is valid six months, renewable once for a year total

faqs.question: How long can I stay in Curaçao?
faqs.answer: Six months initially, renewable once for another six — up to a year total. It's a temporary permit, not a path to permanent residency.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Curaçao?
faqs.answer: No local income tax on your foreign-earned income under the @HOME program. You may still owe tax in your home country depending on citizenship.

faqs.question: What does it cost?
faqs.answer: About ANG 535 (roughly $300) for the application, which is done entirely online.

faqs.question: What income do I need?
faqs.answer: Around €2,600/month (about $2,800), verifiable, from foreign sources.

records.renewal_note: Six months, renewable once for another six — one year in total, then you leave or move to a different permit. @HOME is a temporary-stay permit by design and leads nowhere onward. Dependants can come, but everyone aged 12 and over files their own application.
records.tax_note: @HOME holders owe no Curaçao income tax on foreign-earned income for the duration of the permit. Since the permit itself caps at a year, this is a clean twelve months rather than a long-term arrangement — and the Dutch Caribbean tax position changes entirely if you later move onto an ordinary residence permit.
records.family_note: Dependants can come, but note the mechanics: every family member aged 12 or over files their own separate application rather than being added to yours. Budget the extra time and fees per head.

records.summary: Cyprus offers an English-friendly, sunny EU base with over 300 days of sunshine and a low-crime, low-cost lifestyle by Western-European standards. The Migration Department runs the scheme for non-EU remote workers, with a clear €3,500/month net income bar. The main catch is a hard cap on the number of permits issued, so it can close to new applicants — apply when the window is open.
requirements: Stable net income of at least €3,500/month (after taxes and contributions), from sources outside Cyprus
Be a non-EU / non-EEA national; the scheme is for third-country nationals only
Work remotely — employed by a company registered abroad, or providing services to clients/companies located abroad
Valid passport and proof of accommodation in Cyprus
Private health insurance covering inpatient and outpatient care
Clean criminal record certificate
Completed application submitted to the Migration Department
steps: Check the permit cap is open — Cyprus limits the number of digital nomad permits and applications pause when full
Confirm you meet the €3,500/month net income test from foreign sources
Gather documents: passport, bank statements, employment or client contracts, health insurance, criminal record, proof of accommodation
Submit your application to the Civil Registry and Migration Department (in Nicosia) and pay the fees (about €70 application + €70 registration)
Examination takes roughly 5–7 weeks; the permit is valid one year and renewable for up to two more

faqs.question: Is there a limit on how many people get the Cyprus visa?
faqs.answer: Yes. Cyprus caps the total number of digital nomad permits, and the ceiling has been raised over time as demand grew. When the cap is reached, applications pause until it's increased again — so if the scheme is open, it's worth applying promptly rather than waiting.

faqs.question: Can I bring my family to Cyprus?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your spouse and minor children can join you, but they receive residence permits that don't grant the right to work or carry out economic activity in Cyprus. You'll need to show additional income to support them.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Cyprus?
faqs.answer: If you stay more than 183 days you generally become a Cyprus tax resident. Cyprus has favourable rules, including a 'non-dom' regime, but how your foreign income is treated depends on your situation — confirm with a Cyprus tax adviser before a long stay.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: The initial permit is valid for one year and can be renewed for up to two additional years, for three years total. After that you'd need to look at other Cyprus residency routes.

records.renewal_note: One year, renewable for two more — three years total, then this route is finished and staying means switching to a different immigration category. Renew through the Civil Registry and Migration Department in Nicosia at least a month before expiry (€70). EU long-term residence needs five years of legal residence, which this permit alone cannot get you to.
records.tax_note: Cyprus is unusual twice over. First, the 60-day rule: spend just 60 days here, spend under 183 in any other single country, and keep a permanent home and business ties, and you can be tax resident — and since 1 January 2026 that route no longer requires you to be non-resident elsewhere. Second, non-dom status gives 0% on dividends and interest (and, from 1 January 2026, rental income) for up to 17 years. Read the limit carefully though: non-dom exempts passive income, NOT employment or self-employment earnings, which is what most nomads actually live on. The visa and tax residency are separate applications.

records.summary: Czechia's nomad route is narrower than most: a fast-tracked programme for IT professionals and freelancers from a shortlist of countries, layered on the classic long-stay framework Prague's expats have used for years. If you qualify, you get one of Europe's best cities at half the Western European burn rate.
requirements: Citizenship of an eligible country (includes the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan)
Work in IT or a comparable in-demand field, as an employee of a foreign company or a freelancer
Income/funds around 1.5 times the Czech average gross salary — verify the current figure
University degree or relevant professional experience
Accommodation in Czechia, health insurance, and clean criminal record
steps: Check eligibility (nationality + profession) against the official programme criteria
Apply to the programme for inclusion; freelancers may also need the trade license (živnostenské oprávnění)
Submit the long-stay visa application at the Czech embassy with the programme confirmation
Enter Czechia, register with the foreign police, and renew via a long-term residence permit if staying on

faqs.question: What if I'm not in IT or from an eligible country?
faqs.answer: The classic route still exists: the Czech freelance long-stay visa via a trade license (the 'živno'), open to more professions and nationalities but slower and more bureaucratic. Many Prague nomads have used it for years.

faqs.question: How are freelancers taxed in Czechia?
faqs.answer: Czech freelancers benefit from generous lump-sum expense deductions that can keep effective tax rates low. Once you're tax resident, get a local accountant — the setup is genuinely favorable but paperwork-sensitive.

faqs.question: Does the Czech route lead to permanent residency?
faqs.answer: Yes — unlike pure visa programmes, time on Czech long-term residence permits counts toward permanent residency at five years.

records.renewal_note: One year first, then renewable as a two-year residence permit. Unlike most nomad visas this one sits on the živno (trade licence) track, so the time does count toward the five years needed for permanent residency and ten for citizenship. The catch is at the door, not the exit: the programme is open only to citizens of Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Taiwan, the UK and the US.
records.tax_note: No nomad-specific tax break — the Digital Nomad Programme is an immigration fast-track, not a tax scheme. Over 183 days in a year, or establishing a permanent home here, makes you a Czech tax resident on worldwide income under progressive rates. If you are on the živno track you will also be dealing with Czech social and health contributions as a self-employed person, which people routinely forget to budget for.

records.summary: Ecuador packs the Andes, Amazon, Pacific coast, and the Galápagos into a compact, US-dollar economy with a low cost of living. Its digital nomad visa asks for a modest ~$1,446/month, doesn't tax foreign income, and leads to up to two years of legal residency. You apply from a consulate before you arrive.
records.income_original: $1,446 per month (3× the Ecuadorian minimum wage)
requirements: Monthly income of at least $1,446 (three Unified Basic Salaries), shown for the three months before applying
Remote work as an employee, freelancer, or business owner based outside Ecuador
Valid passport (6+ months validity)
Health insurance with coverage in Ecuador
Clean criminal record
steps: Confirm your income meets the ~$1,446/month threshold over the prior three months
Gather documents: passport, proof of foreign income/employment, health insurance, criminal record
Book a visa appointment at an Ecuadorian embassy or consulate — you must apply before entering Ecuador
Attend the appointment to verify your identity and documents, and pay the visa fees (about $450)
Receive the visa, valid 12 months and renewable for a second year (two years total)

faqs.question: Digital Nomad Visa or Professional Visa?
faqs.answer: If you hold a bachelor's degree, Ecuador's Professional Visa qualifies you at a much lower ~$482/month from any lawful income. Without a degree, working remotely for a foreign employer, the Digital Nomad Visa's ~$1,446/month applies.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Ecuador?
faqs.answer: No — holders aren't liable for Ecuadorian tax on income earned outside the country, a strong draw for remote workers.

faqs.question: Do I apply before arriving?
faqs.answer: Yes. You must apply at an Ecuadorian consulate in your country of residence before entering Ecuador; it's not an on-arrival visa.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: 12 months initially, renewable for another year — up to two years on the digital nomad visa.

records.renewal_note: Two years, renewable in two-year blocks for as long as you still qualify — and unusually among nomad routes, it genuinely settles you. Permanent residency opens at 21 months of physical residence, and naturalisation after roughly three further years of permanent residency. The constraint is presence, not paperwork: as a temporary resident you may be outside Ecuador no more than 90 days per calendar year, and unused days don't roll over. That rules it out as a base for heavy travellers.
records.tax_note: Ecuador taxes territorially: foreign-sourced income is fully exempt, and only Ecuador-source income (local work, local business, rent on Ecuadorian property) is taxed at 0–35%. Combined with the residency route this is the strongest pairing in our dataset — few countries offer both a real path to settlement and no tax on foreign earnings. Document your foreign sourcing properly for the SRI, and remember the flip side of residency: no more than 90 days outside Ecuador per calendar year.

records.summary: El Salvador has reinvented itself as a safe, dollar-denominated, crypto-friendly base with Pacific surf towns and a growing remote-work scene. Its digital nomad visa is accessible at ~$1,460/month, exempts foreign income from tax, and can extend for years. A compact Central American option that's easy to apply for online.
requirements: Monthly income of at least $1,460 for a single applicant (more for dependents), from remote work outside El Salvador
Remote work as an employee, freelancer, or business owner for companies/clients outside El Salvador
Valid passport (valid 6+ months beyond the visa's expiry)
Clean criminal record from every country lived in over the last two years
International health insurance covering your whole stay
steps: Confirm your income meets the ~$1,460/month threshold (higher with dependents)
Gather documents: passport, proof of foreign income, criminal record, health insurance
Apply online, or in person at an El Salvador embassy or consulate (online is usually faster)
Wait for review and approval
Receive the visa; nominally up to two years (currently issued as renewable one-year permits)

faqs.question: How long is the visa valid?
faqs.answer: On paper up to two years, renewable for two more (four years total). In practice the authorities are currently issuing renewable one-year visas.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in El Salvador?
faqs.answer: No — digital nomad visa holders get an exemption from income tax on their foreign earnings.

faqs.question: What's the income requirement?
faqs.answer: About $1,460/month for a single applicant; it rises with dependents — for example, roughly $2,260/month for a couple with one child.

faqs.question: How do I apply?
faqs.answer: Online or through an El Salvador embassy/consulate. Online applications usually have a quicker turnaround.

records.renewal_note: Twelve months to start, and renewable — but by how much is genuinely unclear. Reputable 2026 sources variously describe the ceiling as two, three and four years, and several note that in practice the authorities have been issuing one-year renewals regardless. The residency question is equally muddled: some sources claim eligibility after three consecutive years, others that El Salvador requires five years of continuous residence and that nomad time doesn't qualify. We would rather flag the disagreement than pick a side — confirm with the Dirección General de Migración before planning a long stay.
records.tax_note: El Salvador taxes territorially, so a salary or client income paid from outside the country is not subject to Salvadoran income tax. That is the clearest thing about this programme — as noted above, the renewal and residency rules are considerably less settled.

records.summary: Estonia invented the digital nomad visa, and it remains the most digital-friendly bureaucracy in Europe — the same country that runs e-Residency. The income bar is on the higher side, but the process is clear, fast, and entirely English-friendly, with Tallinn's startup scene as the backdrop.
records.income_original: reputable 2026 sources cite between €3,504 and €4,500 per month
requirements: Remote work for employers or clients registered outside Estonia, or your own foreign company
Gross monthly income above the official threshold (around €4,500) for the six months before applying
Evidence of the work relationship: contracts, payslips, bank statements
Valid travel/health insurance and accommodation plan
Apply at an Estonian embassy or, in some cases, in-country
steps: Confirm you clear the six-month income history at the published threshold
Complete the online application form and book an appointment at the nearest Estonian embassy
Submit documents and biometrics; pay the state fee
Receive the D-visa — up to 12 months, with up to half the time usable across Schengen

faqs.question: Is Estonia's nomad visa connected to e-Residency?
faqs.answer: They're separate things. e-Residency gives you a digital identity to run an Estonian company remotely — it grants no right to live in Estonia. The digital nomad visa is a physical-stay visa. Plenty of nomads combine both: an Estonian company via e-Residency, plus the visa when they want to live there.

faqs.question: Why is Estonia's income requirement so high?
faqs.answer: The threshold tracks Estonian wage statistics and is rechecked periodically, and the country deliberately aims at established remote earners. If you're under it, Croatia and Colombia accept much lower incomes.

faqs.question: Does the Estonian visa lead to residency?
faqs.answer: Not directly — it's a visa, not a residence permit, and it doesn't count toward permanent residency. For a path to staying in Europe long-term, Portugal and Spain are the stronger plays.

records.renewal_note: Estonia's is a visa, not a residence permit — one year maximum, no extension, and time on it counts toward neither permanent residency nor citizenship. You can reapply after a spell outside Estonia. E-Residency is a separate thing entirely and grants no right to live here.
records.tax_note: No nomad-specific break: cross 183 days in any 12-month period and you are an Estonian tax resident, taxed on worldwide income at the flat 22% rate with a €700/month tax-free allowance. Below that threshold you generally aren't resident — which, given the visa maxes out at a year, makes the day count worth tracking deliberately rather than accidentally.
records.logistics_note: Filed at an Estonian embassy or consulate. Two things to plan for. The income test looks backwards over six months rather than at a single payslip, so a recent jump in earnings won't carry an application on its own. And the threshold itself is genuinely disputed — 2026 sources cite figures from €3,504 to €4,500 per month, so confirm the current number with the Police and Border Guard Board before assembling statements.

records.summary: Greece pairs one of Europe's most livable climates with a nomad visa that converts into a two-year renewable residence permit — and a 50% income tax break for those who shift their tax residence there. Athens and Thessaloniki for city life, the islands for everything else.
requirements: Remote work for employers or clients outside Greece — working for Greek companies is not allowed
Monthly net income of at least €3,500 (rises 20% for a spouse, 15% per child)
Employment contract or proof of freelance/business activity
Health insurance, accommodation in Greece, and a clean criminal record
Apply at the Greek consulate in your country of residence
steps: Assemble income proof, contracts, insurance, and accommodation documents
Apply at the Greek consulate — decisions are legally due within 10 days when files are complete
Enter Greece on the 12-month visa
Before it expires, apply in-country for the two-year digital nomad residence permit, renewable while conditions hold

faqs.question: What is Greece's 50% tax incentive for nomads?
faqs.answer: If you move your tax residence to Greece and qualify under the special regime, half of your Greek-taxable employment income can be exempt from income tax for up to seven years. It requires committing to Greek tax residency — get Greek tax advice before counting on it.

faqs.question: Can I visit the rest of Europe on the Greek visa?
faqs.answer: Yes — Greece is in Schengen, so you can move around the zone under the standard 90/180 rules while holding the visa or permit.

faqs.question: Does the Greek nomad permit lead anywhere long-term?
faqs.answer: The permit renews in two-year blocks, but time on it does not count toward permanent residency or citizenship. It's built for staying comfortably, not naturalizing.

records.renewal_note: The 12-month visa converts to a two-year residence permit that keeps renewing while you meet the income and insurance bar. Permanent residency needs five years with more than 183 days a year in Greece; citizenship needs seven, plus B1 Greek and an integration exam. Since February 2026 you must obtain the national (Type D) visa at a consulate first — applying from inside Greece as a tourist was abolished.
records.tax_note: Greece halves it: nomads who move their tax residency here get a 50% exemption on qualifying income for up to seven years. On €60,000 that works out around a 9.83% effective rate. You become tax resident on passing 183 days in a calendar year, at which point Greece taxes worldwide income — the exemption reduces the bill, it doesn't remove the obligation to file.
records.family_note: Family members can be included, with the income requirement rising per person. As in Croatia and Malta, an accompanying spouse's right to work in Greece is restricted, so treat the visa as supporting one remote income rather than two local ones.
records.logistics_note: This changed in February 2026 and older guides are now wrong: you must obtain the national (Type D) visa at a Greek consulate before travelling. Applying from inside Greece as a tourist was abolished by Law 5275/2026. If a guide tells you to fly in and sort it locally, it predates the change.

records.summary: Hungary's White Card gives remote workers a budget-friendly EU base in Budapest — grand architecture, thermal baths, and a low cost of living for the Schengen zone. It asks for €3,000/month income plus savings, runs up to two years, and is straightforward to apply for. One caveat: it's a dead-end for residency — it can't lead to permanent residency or citizenship.
requirements: Net monthly income of at least €3,000 for the six months before applying, maintained during your stay
At least €10,000 in savings
Be a third-country national working remotely for a foreign company or your own business abroad
Comprehensive health insurance (or proof you can cover healthcare costs)
A rental or purchase agreement for accommodation in Hungary (12 months)
Valid passport
steps: Confirm you've earned €3,000+/month net for the last six months and hold €10,000+ in savings
Gather documents: passport, six months of income proof, savings proof, insurance, 12-month accommodation agreement
Visa-free nationals can travel to Hungary and apply for the White Card directly; others apply at a Hungarian consulate first
Submit your application; processing typically takes 21–30 days
Receive the one-year residence permit, extendable once for two years total

faqs.question: Can the White Card lead to permanent residency?
faqs.answer: No. The White Card explicitly does not confer a path to permanent residency or citizenship, and after two years you must leave Hungary. It's for a defined stay, not settling permanently.

faqs.question: Can I work for a Hungarian company?
faqs.answer: No. White Card holders can't work for a Hungarian employer — your income must come from a foreign company or your own business abroad.

faqs.question: What are the financial requirements?
faqs.answer: €3,000/month net income for the prior six months, plus at least €10,000 in savings. You must maintain the income level throughout your stay in Hungary.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: One year, extendable once for the same period — two years maximum. After that, you must leave Hungary.

records.renewal_note: Issued for a year and extendable once — two years is a hard ceiling, and at the end of it you leave. Time on a White Card counts toward nothing: it cannot convert to permanent residence, and the years don't accrue toward it either.
records.tax_note: White Card holders are generally not taxed in Hungary on foreign income — until presence makes them resident. Cross 183 days in a year and you become a Hungarian tax resident, at which point the flat 15% personal income tax applies. Since the card itself is capped at two years and expects you to live here, treat the 183-day line as something you will probably cross rather than an edge case.
records.family_note: The hard no of this dataset. The White Card carries no family reunification at all — a partner and children get no residence permit from your application and must qualify separately on some other basis. Families with school-age children are effectively excluded from this route.

records.summary: Bali finally got a real nomad visa: the E33G remote worker KITAS gives a full year of legal residence (renewable) for remote employees of foreign companies. The income bar is steep at $60,000/year, but it ends the visa-run era for the world's most famous nomad island.
requirements: Employment contract with a company located outside Indonesia
Annual income of at least $60,000, paid into a personal account
Bank statement showing roughly $2,000 in the last 3 months
Passport valid 6+ months; application via the official e-visa portal
No working for Indonesian companies or clients
steps: Prepare employment contract, income proof, bank statement, passport scan
Apply on the official evisa.imigrasi.go.id portal (or via a reputable visa agent — common in Bali)
Pay the fees and receive the e-visa approval
Enter Indonesia and complete the KITAS formalities; renew annually while eligible

faqs.question: What if I don't meet the $60k income bar for the E33G?
faqs.answer: Most nomads use the C1 tourist e-visa (60 days, extendable to 180) and accept periodic resets. There's also the B211A-style social/cultural route via agents. The E33G is for those who want a real KITAS and a Bali base without visa runs.

faqs.question: Do remote workers pay Indonesian tax on the E33G?
faqs.answer: Stay 183+ days and you're technically a tax resident, but Indonesia has signaled that foreign-source income of remote workers on this visa is not its target, and double-tax treaties usually protect employment income taxed at home. The practice is still settling — get advice if you're going full-time.

faqs.question: Does the E33G cover freelancers?
faqs.answer: It's written around employees with a foreign employment contract. Freelancers with multiple clients fit awkwardly — some qualify via their own company employing them; otherwise the tourist-visa pattern remains the fallback.

records.renewal_note: Renewable a year at a time, and under the general one-year ITAS framework the stack can reach around six years. Two caveats worth knowing before you count on it. First, sources disagree on the mechanics — some describe a true in-country extension, others say you must apply for a fresh E33G with new employment and financial evidence each time; budget for the stricter version. Second, converting to KITAP (permanent stay) is not a right: official guidance says an E33G may be converted to another permit when you qualify, which is not the same as the E33G itself leading to permanent residency. Start an extension up to 30 days before expiry; processing runs about 14 working days.
records.tax_note: The common belief that Bali is tax-free on a nomad visa is wrong. Indonesia taxes residents on worldwide income, and holding an E33G KITAS is treated as intent to reside — which can make you a tax resident regardless of your day count. There is a territorial option (PMK-18/2021) covering only Indonesian-sourced income for your first four fiscal years, but it is limited to foreigners with 'particular expertise' in science, technology or mathematics, and it must be formally applied for. It is not automatic and most remote workers won't qualify.
records.family_note: Indonesia runs a dedicated family-dependent visa for remote workers covering a spouse and children, applied for alongside the E33G rather than bundled into it.
records.logistics_note: Filed through Indonesia's online immigration system. Renewals are handled in-country, though sources disagree on whether that is a true extension or a fresh application each time — budget for the stricter reading.

records.summary: Italy's long-awaited nomad visa finally arrived in 2024, aimed at 'highly skilled' remote workers. The income bar is moderate by European standards, the visa renews annually, and the prize is living in Italy — the paperwork is heavier than its neighbors, but that's the Italian deal across the board.
requirements: Qualify as highly skilled: a university degree, professional accreditation, or substantial professional experience
At least six months of prior experience in the remote work you'll be doing
Annual income of at least about €28,000 (consulates apply €25,000–30,000 depending on profile)
Health insurance covering Italy, accommodation proof, and a clean criminal record
No conviction-related bars for the employer/company if you're employed
steps: Confirm you meet the highly-skilled definition and income threshold
Book the appointment at the Italian consulate for your residence country and submit the dossier
Enter Italy on the visa, then apply for the residence permit (permesso di soggiorno) at the post office/questura within 8 working days
Renew annually while the conditions continue to hold

faqs.question: Who counts as 'highly skilled' for Italy's nomad visa?
faqs.answer: Broadly: a degree, a recognized professional qualification, or strong documented professional experience in your field. Consulates assess this case by case — bring more evidence than you think you need.

faqs.question: Will I pay Italian taxes?
faqs.answer: Spend over 183 days a year in Italy and you become a tax resident on worldwide income. Italy has a reduced 'impatriate' regime that can significantly cut taxable income for new residents who qualify — worth a consultation before you move.

faqs.question: Can my family come with me to Italy?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can accompany or join you under family-cohesion rules, with income requirements scaled up accordingly.

records.renewal_note: The permesso di soggiorno runs up to a year and renews annually while you still meet the income, insurance and accommodation conditions. Five continuous years earns EU long-term resident status; ten earns citizenship.
records.tax_note: Italy's impatriati regime exempts 50% of employment or professional income for five years (60% with a dependent child under 18), capped at €600,000 — but read the eligibility before counting on it. You must have been non-resident for the previous three years, hold a degree or qualify as highly skilled, and work mainly in Italy. Crucially it covers employment and professional income and EXCLUDES business and freelance income, which rules out a large share of nomads. A dedicated digital-nomad incentive has been proposed in the 2026 budget process but is not law.
records.logistics_note: Visa at the consulate first, then apply for the permesso di soggiorno within eight days of arriving in Italy. That eight-day window is the step people miss.

records.summary: Japan's 2024 nomad visa is short and demanding — six months, no renewal, ¥10 million yearly income — but it's six legal months in Japan, which tourist entries never reliably gave remote workers. For high earners who've always wanted a Tokyo or Kyoto season, this is the clean way to do it.
requirements: Annual income of at least ¥10 million (roughly $65,000–70,000 depending on exchange rate)
Citizenship of one of ~50 eligible countries/regions (visa-waiver countries with tax treaties — US, UK, EU members, Australia, etc.)
Remote work for employers/clients outside Japan
Private health insurance covering the stay (death/injury/illness, ¥10M+ coverage)
Spouse and children can accompany you under a linked status
steps: Confirm nationality eligibility and the income bar
Prepare income evidence, insurance certificate, and the activity description
Apply for the Certificate of Eligibility / visa at the Japanese embassy
Enter Japan with 'designated activities' status — 6 months, non-extendable; reapply after at least 6 months outside Japan

faqs.question: Can I extend the Japan nomad visa or convert it to residency?
faqs.answer: No — six months is the ceiling, it doesn't renew, and it grants no residence card or path to longer status. You can apply again after spending six months outside Japan. It's built for seasons, not settling.

faqs.question: Do I pay Japanese taxes during the six months?
faqs.answer: Generally no — under six months you typically remain a non-resident, and the eligible-country list was built around tax treaties precisely to keep remote income taxed at home. Keep your stay within the visa term and ordinary cases stay clean.

faqs.question: Why can't I just do this on a tourist entry?
faqs.answer: Japan's tourist status doesn't authorize work, even remote work for foreign employers — it's a grey zone people used quietly. The nomad visa makes the same stay legal, insurable, and honest on landing cards.

records.renewal_note: Six months, flatly non-extendable — when it expires you leave, and a cooling-off period (widely reported as six months outside Japan) applies before you can apply again. You are not issued a residence card (zairyu card), which is the tell: this is a long visitor permission rather than residence, and it builds nothing toward permanent residency.
records.tax_note: The visa's six-month cap and the tax line are designed to agree: stay 183 days or fewer, be paid by a foreign employer with no Japanese branch, and Japan treats you as non-resident and does not tax that foreign income. Because the visa cannot be extended past six months, you are structurally unlikely to cross into residency — which is arguably the programme's main appeal, given how heavily Japan taxes residents on worldwide income.
records.family_note: Unusually generous on paper: a spouse and children can be included on the same application and Japan does not require extra income for them, unlike most European programmes. Two conditions people miss — children must be unmarried and under 19, and your dependants must themselves be nationals of visa-exempt countries.
records.logistics_note: Applied for at a Japanese consulate before travelling, and because the visa cannot be extended you will be doing this from outside Japan again if you return. No residence card is issued, which affects everyday admin such as opening a bank account or signing a phone contract.

records.summary: Latvia offers an affordable EU base with a digital, fast-internet capital in Riga, Baltic coastline, and easy Schengen travel. Its digital nomad visa is open only to people working for — or self-employed in — OECD-country companies, with a high income bar of about €4,213/month. For OECD-tied remote workers wanting an EU foothold for up to two years, it's a clean option.
records.income_original: cited between €3,400 and roughly €4,200 per month
requirements: Monthly income of at least €4,213 (about 2.5× Latvia's average salary)
Employment by, or self-employment registered in, an OECD member country — the defining condition of this visa
Be a third-country national (non-EU/EEA/Swiss)
At least six months of consistent remote-work history
Health insurance valid in Latvia and the Schengen area (minimum €42,600 coverage)
Proof of accommodation in Latvia
steps: Confirm you work for (or are self-employed in) an OECD country and meet the €4,213/month income bar
Gather documents: passport, six months of income proof, OECD employer/registration proof, insurance, accommodation
File the long-stay visa application at a Latvian mission abroad (often via VFS Global) or the PMLP e-form
A decision is normally made within 10–15 business days (up to 60 if more information is needed)
Receive the one-year visa, extendable for a second year (two years total)

faqs.question: What's the OECD requirement?
faqs.answer: Latvia's nomad visa is only open to people employed by, or self-employed and registered in, an OECD member country. You'll prove this via your employer's registration or an OECD tax authority confirmation — it's the key eligibility filter.

faqs.question: How much income do I need?
faqs.answer: About €4,213/month, roughly 2.5 times Latvia's average gross salary — one of the higher European thresholds. It must be shown over the prior six months.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: One year, renewable for a second, for two years total. After that you must spend at least six months outside Latvia before reapplying.

faqs.question: Can I work for a Latvian company?
faqs.answer: No. The visa doesn't grant the right to local employment — your income must come from your OECD-based employer or clients.

records.renewal_note: One year, renewable once, two years maximum. Be careful with the claim — common on nomad sites — that this converts to permanent residency at two years: Latvia's DNV is a long-stay visa rather than a residence permit, and Latvian permanent residence normally requires five years of continuous residence on a permit. Sources disagree, so treat the PR route as unconfirmed and ask the OCMA directly. Eligibility is also narrower than most: you must work for an employer or own a business registered in an OECD country.
records.tax_note: We could not find a published nomad-specific tax exemption here, and we are not going to assume one exists — nor assume it doesn't. What is solid: residents are taxed on worldwide income, and passing 183 days in a year normally makes you resident. Confirm the current position with the national tax authority before you plan around it.
records.logistics_note: Filed at a Latvian embassy or consulate, and eligibility is narrower than most: you must work for an employer or own a business registered in an OECD country. The income threshold is tied to a multiple of the Latvian average wage and therefore moves — published 2026 figures disagree by several hundred euros, so treat any single number as indicative and confirm with the OCMA.

records.summary: Malaysia's DE Rantau pass is Southeast Asia's most accessible nomad visa: $24,000/year income for digital professionals, 12 months renewable for another 12, and Kuala Lumpur's first-world infrastructure at developing-world prices. Penang and Langkawi are certified 'nomad hubs' with vetted housing and workspaces.
records.income_original: $24,000 per year (tech roles) or $60,000 per year (non-tech)
requirements: Work in a digital field: IT, software, content, digital marketing, design, and similar (non-IT professionals have a higher income bar)
Annual income of at least $24,000 for digital/IT applicants — verify the current threshold for your category
Active employment contract (3+ months remaining) or freelance contracts with foreign or local clients
Passport valid 14+ months, proof of income (bank statements/payslips), personal bond payment
Health insurance covering Malaysia for you and any dependents
steps: Check your professional category and income threshold on the MDEC DE Rantau portal
Apply online with contracts, income proof, resume, and passport documents
Pay the pass and processing fees once conditionally approved
Receive the pass, enter Malaysia, and renew once for a second year if still eligible

faqs.question: Can I work for Malaysian clients on DE Rantau?
faqs.answer: Yes — unusually, DE Rantau allows freelancers to serve local Malaysian clients as well as foreign ones. Most nomad visas prohibit local work entirely; this is one of the pass's quiet advantages.

faqs.question: Can I bring family on the DE Rantau pass?
faqs.answer: Yes — spouse and children can come as dependents with additional fees per person. KL's international schools and healthcare make it one of Asia's easiest family-nomad setups.

faqs.question: Do I pay Malaysian tax as a DE Rantau holder?
faqs.answer: Malaysia generally does not tax foreign-source income remitted by individuals under current exemptions, and short-stay nomads rarely trigger issues. Cross 182 days and you're tax resident — usually still benign for foreign income, but confirm the current rules.

records.renewal_note: Twelve months, renewable once — 24 months total. Renewal is discretionary rather than automatic; apply two months before expiry and expect six to eight weeks of processing. The pass is issued as a Professional Visit Pass, a category built for temporary stay, so it does not move you toward permanent residence.
records.tax_note: Malaysia taxes territorially and foreign-sourced income received by individuals is generally exempt — the reason DE Rantau looks so attractive on tax. Watch the expiry date, because it has moved: the individual exemption was previously running out on 31 December 2026, and Budget 2026 extended it to 31 December 2036. Confirm the current position with LHDN before relying on it, since this is precisely the kind of provision that gets revisited.
records.family_note: DE Rantau covers a dependent spouse and children. The pass fee is charged per head — roughly RM1,000 for the main applicant and RM500 per dependant.
records.logistics_note: Filed online through the DE Rantau portal run by MDEC. Note the two-tier income test — tech and non-tech applicants face very different bars for the same pass.

records.summary: Malta pairs an English-speaking, year-round-sunny Mediterranean base with one of Europe's most generous nomad tax deals: a flat 10% on foreign remote-work income once you're tax resident, and a full exemption in your first year. The Residency Malta Agency runs the permit directly, you can apply without an agent, and holding it gives you Schengen travel. The trade-off is a higher income bar than most and a small-island cost of living.
requirements: Gross income of at least €42,000/year (about €3,500/month), from active remote work — savings and investments don't count toward the threshold
Be a third-country national (non-EU/EEA/Swiss); EU citizens don't need this permit
Remote work in one of three forms: employment with a foreign-registered company, ownership of a foreign company, or freelance/consulting for clients based abroad
Valid rental or purchase agreement for property in Malta
Health insurance covering risks in Malta and across the EU
Clean police conduct certificate
Valid passport and completed background verification
steps: Confirm you qualify on income (€42,000/year gross) and the third-country-national rule
Line up Maltese accommodation — a rental or purchase agreement is required for the application
Gather documents: passport, three months of bank statements and payslips, work contract, health insurance, police conduct certificate
Submit the application directly to the Residency Malta Agency and pay the fees (about €300 application + €100 residence card)
On approval (around 30 days), collect your residence card; the permit is valid one year and renewable up to four years total

faqs.question: How does Malta's 10% nomad tax actually work?
faqs.answer: If you spend more than 183 days in Malta you become tax resident, and foreign-sourced remote-work income is taxed at a flat 10% rather than Malta's normal progressive rates. In your first year on the permit, that foreign income is exempt entirely. You may still have home-country obligations depending on your citizenship, so confirm with a cross-border accountant.

faqs.question: Can EU citizens use the Malta Nomad Residence Permit?
faqs.answer: No — it's only for third-country nationals (non-EU, non-EEA, non-Swiss). EU/EEA/Swiss citizens already have the right to live and work in Malta and don't need this permit.

faqs.question: Can I bring my family?
faqs.answer: Yes. Spouses and dependent children can be added to your application. You'll need to show additional income to support each dependent and provide their documents, but they're covered under the same permit framework.

faqs.question: How long can I stay on the permit?
faqs.answer: The permit is issued for one year and can be renewed up to three more times, for a maximum of four years. Renewals depend on continuing to meet the income and eligibility requirements at each step.

records.renewal_note: Renewable three times, four years maximum, then it stops — Residency Malta states plainly that this permit leads to neither permanent residency nor citizenship. Each renewal wants bank statements proving you actually spent at least five months of the previous twelve in Malta.
records.tax_note: Nomad Residence Permit holders get a 12-month exemption from Maltese income tax on authorised work income, then a flat 10% from year two — against standard rates reaching 35%. The Malta Tax & Customs Administration formally clarified this in January 2026. Note the mechanism: the 10% applies to income remitted to Malta, so how and when you bring money in matters as much as what you earn.
records.family_note: Dependants are allowed and Malta is one of the more family-workable options in Europe — but a spouse's right to work locally is restricted, so plan on the household running on remote income only.
records.logistics_note: Handled online through the Residency Malta Agency rather than at a consulate — one of the more administratively straightforward programmes in Europe. Budget around 60 days for processing.

records.summary: Mauritius is a tropical Indian Ocean base — beaches, a stable economy, and English widely spoken — with one of the most accessible nomad visas anywhere. The Premium Visa has a low $1,500/month income bar, is completely free, and is often approved within about a week. Valid a year and renewable, it's a low-friction way to live and work remotely in paradise.
requirements: Minimum income of $1,500/month for a single applicant ($3,000 for a couple; +$500/month per child under 24)
