Remote work for an employer or clients based outside Mauritius
Valid passport
Travel or health insurance covering the duration of your stay
No intention to work in the Mauritian labour market or do business with Mauritius residents
steps: Confirm your income meets the $1,500/month minimum (more for dependents)
Gather documents: passport, proof of remote income, travel/health insurance, travel plans
Apply online through the Mauritius Premium Visa portal — there's no application fee
Receive approval, often within about a week
Enter on the multi-entry Premium Visa, valid one year and renewable

faqs.question: How much does the Mauritius Premium Visa cost?
faqs.answer: Nothing. The application is free of charge with no government processing fee — which, combined with the low income bar, makes it one of the most accessible nomad visas available.

faqs.question: How long does approval take?
faqs.answer: Often very fast — approval can come in as little as about a week, much quicker than most European nomad visas.

faqs.question: Will I be taxed in Mauritius?
faqs.answer: Money you keep offshore generally isn't taxed in Mauritius, but income remitted into the country can be. Mauritius has relatively low taxes overall — confirm your specific situation with a local adviser if you stay long-term.

faqs.question: Can I bring my family?
faqs.answer: Yes. A spouse and dependent children can be included, with the income requirement rising for each — about $3,000/month for a couple and an extra $500/month per child.

records.renewal_note: One year, renewable, and unusually there is no published cap on how many times — holders describe renewing with substantially the same paperwork each time. Note what it is, though: Mauritius issues this as a premium *travel* visa rather than a residence permit, so it should not be assumed to accrue toward permanent residence. Mauritius has separate residence and occupation permit routes for that.
records.tax_note: Mauritius does have a personal income tax, but it works on a remittance basis for foreign income: only what you actually bring into Mauritius is taxable there. In practice that produces a near-zero outcome for many Premium Visa holders — but it is an outcome you have to manage, not an automatic exemption, so how and when you remit money is the whole question.
records.logistics_note: One of the fastest in the dataset — approvals have been reported in as little as seven days, against the 60-plus days common in Europe.

records.summary: Mexico never created a dedicated nomad visa — it didn't need one. The Temporary Resident Visa gives remote workers up to four years of legal residence on an income or savings test, and Mexico City, Oaxaca, and the coasts already host one of the world's largest nomad populations.
requirements: Proof of solvency: monthly income (roughly $4,000–4,500, consulates vary) over the last 6 months, OR savings around $70,000+ over 12 months
Application starts at a Mexican consulate outside Mexico — requirements and thresholds genuinely differ by consulate
Valid passport and consulate-specific documentation
After entry, exchange the visa for the resident card at the INM office within 30 days
Remote income from abroad; working for Mexican employers requires work permission
steps: Pick your consulate strategically — thresholds and appetite vary; book the appointment
Present income/savings statements, passport, photos at the interview
Receive the visa, enter Mexico within 180 days
Complete the canje at INM within 30 days of entry to get your 1-year resident card
Renew in-country for up to 3 more years, then convert to permanent residency

faqs.question: Why do requirements differ between Mexican consulates?
faqs.answer: Consulates apply the financial criteria with real discretion — minimums, documents, even whether they accept remote-work cases vary. Nomad forums track which consulates are currently straightforward; check recent reports before booking.

faqs.question: Can I stay in Mexico as a tourist instead?
faqs.answer: Tourist entries (FMM) can grant up to 180 days, but immigration officers increasingly stamp fewer days, and back-to-back tourist runs draw scrutiny. For anything beyond a season, temporary residency is the durable answer.

faqs.question: Does temporary residency lead to permanent status?
faqs.answer: Yes — after four years of temporary residency (or two if married to a Mexican citizen) you can convert to permanent residency, which has no renewal requirement.

records.renewal_note: Issued for one year, then renewable for one, two or three more — four years total as a temporary resident, after which you can convert to permanent residency. This is one of the few nomad-friendly routes that genuinely settles you: naturalisation needs five years of legal residence immediately before applying and temporary-resident time counts toward it, or just two years for nationals of Latin American countries, Spain and Portugal. Expect a Spanish language and Mexican history exam.
records.tax_note: No nomad-specific break. Mexico taxes residents on worldwide income at progressive rates, and residency turns less on a day count than on where your 'centre of vital interests' sits — establishing a home and life here can make you resident even without an obvious 183-day trigger. If you take the four-year temporary-residency route seriously, assume you will be filing in Mexico.
records.family_note: A spouse and children can accompany you, with a higher income threshold and extra paperwork — marriage and birth certificates, generally apostilled. Mexico's family-unity provisions are well-trodden, which makes this one of the more predictable family routes in the dataset.

records.summary: Montenegro packs Adriatic coastline, mountains, and a low cost of living into a small, scenic Balkan country. Its digital nomad visa allows up to four years total and exempts your foreign income from local tax. One important caveat: the program is currently scheduled to end on 31 December 2026, so confirm it's still open before you plan around it.
requirements: Remote income above roughly 3× Montenegro's minimum wage — in 2026, about €1,800/month (vocational) or €2,400/month (bachelor's degree or higher)
Proof of remote work for an employer or clients outside Montenegro (employer letter or client contracts)
Valid passport
Health insurance valid in Montenegro
A rental agreement for accommodation in Montenegro
Clean criminal record, certified and translated into Montenegrin
steps: Check the program is still open — it's currently scheduled to end 31 December 2026
Confirm your income clears the threshold for your education level (~€1,800 or ~€2,400/month)
Gather documents: passport, proof of remote work, health insurance, rental agreement, translated criminal record
Apply through Montenegro's official portal at digitalnomads.gov.me
Processing runs about 9–12 weeks; the permit allows up to 2 years, renewable once for 4 years total

faqs.question: Is the Montenegro nomad visa ending?
faqs.answer: As of 2026 the program is scheduled to end on 31 December 2026. It may be extended, but confirm its status on the official portal before making plans — don't assume it'll still be open later in the year.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax on the visa?
faqs.answer: No — digital nomad visa holders are exempt from Montenegrin income tax on foreign earnings. You may still owe tax in your home country depending on your citizenship and time abroad.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: The permit allows up to two years and can be renewed once for another two, for four years maximum. After the four years you must leave for six months before reapplying.

faqs.question: How do I apply?
faqs.answer: Through the official government portal at digitalnomads.gov.me. The full process — from consultation to residence permit — typically takes 9–12 weeks.

records.renewal_note: Up to two years, renewable once — four years maximum, and then it ends. The part that catches people: those four years count for nothing toward permanent residence, which needs five continuous years of ordinary temporary residence. If settling is the goal you have to switch to a standard route (company, property, employment, family) early rather than late. Note too that the programme itself is currently legislated only to 31 December 2026, with no extension confirmed — anyone planning around it should confirm the scheme still exists before committing.
records.tax_note: We could not find a published nomad-specific tax exemption here, and we are not going to assume one exists — nor assume it doesn't. What is solid: residents are taxed on worldwide income, and passing 183 days in a year normally makes you resident. Confirm the current position with the national tax authority before you plan around it.

records.summary: Namibia offers dramatic desert-and-safari landscapes, English as the official language, and solid connectivity in Windhoek and Swakopmund — a striking, low-cost African base. Its digital nomad visa is straightforward at $2,000/month income, though it caps at six months with no renewal and requires a chest X-ray as part of the process. Best for a defined half-year stay rather than a long-term move.
requirements: Income of at least $2,000/month for the main applicant ($1,000 for a spouse, $500 per child), from payslips or contracts — savings don't count
Proof of remote employment or client contracts, plus a portfolio of work
Six months of bank statements
Health insurance valid in Namibia
A radiological report (chest X-ray) by a licensed radiologist — a standard Namibian immigration requirement
Original or notarised police clearance from your home country (translated if not in English)
steps: Confirm your income meets the $2,000/month threshold (it must come from work, not savings)
Complete application form 3-1/0033 (and a separate form for any dependents)
Get your chest X-ray (radiological report) and police clearance certificate
Submit the application by email to the NIPDB before you travel
On approval, enter Namibia and pay the NAD 3,300 fee (about $180) on arrival; the visa is valid six months, non-renewable

faqs.question: Why do I need a chest X-ray?
faqs.answer: A radiological report (chest X-ray) by a licensed radiologist is a standard requirement under Namibian immigration rules and must be included with your application — one of the more unusual documents among nomad visas.

faqs.question: How long can I stay in Namibia?
faqs.answer: Six months total. The visa is not renewable, so once it expires you must leave the country. It's designed for a defined half-year stay, not long-term relocation.

faqs.question: Where do I apply?
faqs.answer: Through the Namibia Investment Promotion and Development Board (NIPDB), by email, before you arrive. You pay the NAD 3,300 (about $180) fee on arrival in Namibia.

faqs.question: Can my family join me?
faqs.answer: Yes. Dependents complete a separate form, and the income requirement rises — about $1,000/month for a spouse and $500/month per child on top of your own income.

records.renewal_note: Six months, not renewable — and the cooling-off is unusually harsh: you may only reapply 12 months after your previous visa expired, so a second stint means a full year away. Plan it as a single six-month season rather than a base.
records.tax_note: No published nomad-specific tax treatment that we could verify. In practice the six-month, non-renewable design means most holders will not be there long enough to trigger residency — but confirm with the Namibia Revenue Agency rather than assuming, particularly if you already have Namibian ties.
records.family_note: Dependants are allowed and the tiers are published plainly: $2,000/month alone, $3,000 with a spouse, $3,500 with a spouse and one dependant, then a further $500 per additional dependant.

records.summary: Panama is the easy on-ramp to Latin America for remote workers — a US-dollar economy, fast Caribbean and Pacific access, and a modern, connected base in Panama City. The short-stay remote worker visa (the country's digital nomad route) asks for solid income and must be filed through a local lawyer, but Panama's territorial tax system means your foreign income isn't taxed here. Best for a 9-to-18-month stay rather than settling.
requirements: Foreign-source income of at least $36,000/year ($3,000/month), from an employer or clients outside Panama
A work contract with a foreign company, or proof of self-employed remote work for clients abroad
Private health insurance valid in Panama for the stay
Valid passport with at least six months' validity and three passport photos
Clean criminal background certificate
A licensed Panamanian immigration lawyer to file the application — you can't submit directly
steps: Confirm you meet the $36,000/year foreign-income requirement
Engage a licensed Panamanian immigration lawyer — filing through one is legally required
Gather documents: passport, bank statements, work/client contracts, health insurance, criminal record
Your lawyer files with the Servicio Nacional de Migración and pays the fees (~$250 + $50 card)
On approval (about 30–45 business days), receive the 9-month visa, renewable once for 18 months total

faqs.question: Why do I need a lawyer to apply?
faqs.answer: Panama law requires immigration applications to be filed by a licensed Panamanian attorney — you can't submit the remote worker visa directly to immigration yourself. Budget for legal fees on top of the roughly $300 in government charges.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Panama?
faqs.answer: Not on foreign income. Panama uses a territorial tax system, so income earned from sources outside Panama isn't taxed locally — a major draw of this visa. You may still owe tax in your home country depending on your citizenship.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: The visa is granted for nine months and can be renewed once for another nine, for a maximum of 18 months. It's a short-stay route, not a path to permanent residency.

faqs.question: Can I bring my family?
faqs.answer: Dependents can generally be included with additional documentation and income evidence. Confirm the current per-dependent requirements with your immigration lawyer.

records.renewal_note: Nine months, extendable once by another nine — 18 months maximum, then the route is finished. It is explicitly a non-resident permit: it establishes neither tax residency nor immigration residency, and no amount of it counts toward permanent residency or citizenship. Panama has plenty of routes that do settle you (Friendly Nations, Qualified Investor); this is not one of them.
records.tax_note: Panama taxes territorially — income earned outside Panama is not subject to Panamanian income tax — and the remote-worker visa is explicitly a non-resident permit that does not establish tax residency at all. That combination is why the 18-month cap stings: the tax treatment is about as clean as it gets, and it expires.

records.summary: Peru wrote a digital nomad residence category into law, but as of mid-2026 the application procedure has never been published — there is no way to apply, no official fees, and no launch date. Ignore any site walking you through a Peru nomad visa 'application'; it doesn't exist yet. The good news: nomads live in Peru anyway, on generous tourist stays of up to 183 days a year, with the independent-worker residence route for those who want to stay formally.
requirements: Status check (verified July 2026): the nomad-visa category exists in law but Migraciones has not published the procedure — applications are not open
Announced-but-unconfirmed criteria if it launches: roughly US$2,500/month of remote income earned from employers or clients outside Peru
Remote work only — the category as written prohibits working for Peruvian companies or earning locally
What you actually need today: a passport most nationalities can use to enter visa-free as a tourist, with the officer granting up to 183 days per year
steps: Today's realistic route: enter as a tourist — most Western passports are visa-free — and ask for the maximum stay; officers can grant up to 183 days in a rolling year
Work remotely for foreign clients on that tourist stay, as most nomads in Lima, Cusco, and Arequipa currently do; keep foreign income and local work strictly separate
Want formal, renewable status? Look at the trabajador independiente (independent worker) residence route with a Peruvian immigration lawyer
If the nomad-visa procedure ever goes live, apply through Migraciones (migraciones.gob.pe) — check its TUPA updates for the category being switched on

faqs.question: Can I apply for Peru's digital nomad visa now?
faqs.answer: No. The category was created in law and regulations were even approved, but successive updates to the official procedures came and went without the application process ever being published. As of mid-2026 there is no form, no fee schedule, and no way to file. Any website offering to 'walk you through the application' is describing a visa that cannot currently be obtained.

faqs.question: How do digital nomads stay in Peru legally then?
faqs.answer: As tourists. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free and immigration officers can grant up to 183 days in a rolling year — one of the longest tourist allowances anywhere, and enough for a serious stint in Lima or Cusco. Working remotely for foreign employers on a tourist stay is the de facto norm; what's prohibited is working for Peruvian companies or earning income locally.

faqs.question: What income would the visa require if it launches?
faqs.answer: The announced figure attached to the category is roughly US$2,500 per month of remote income from outside Peru, provable via bank statements, contracts, or an employer letter — but since the procedure was never published, no figure is operational. Treat it as a signal of intent, not a requirement you can plan around, and verify with Migraciones if the category ever opens.

faqs.question: Is there any formal residence route for remote workers today?
faqs.answer: The nearest thing is the trabajador independiente (independent-worker) residence, aimed at freelancers and contractors who can document their income. It's a real, renewable status — but it's paperwork-heavy and typically worth doing with a Peruvian immigration lawyer. For stays under six months a year, the tourist allowance is simpler and what nearly everyone uses.

records.summary: Portugal's D8 visa is the European benchmark for nomads who want to settle rather than pass through: prove solid remote income, and it converts into a renewable residence permit with a path to permanent residency and citizenship. Mild winters, strong nomad communities in Lisbon, Porto, and Madeira, and full Schengen access while you hold it.
requirements: Remote income of at least four times the Portuguese minimum wage per month, earned from employers or clients outside Portugal
Proof of accommodation in Portugal (rental contract, booking, or invitation letter)
Portuguese tax number (NIF) — obtainable remotely through a fiscal representative
Savings buffer — banks and consulates typically want to see roughly a year of minimum-wage equivalent in reserve
Clean criminal record certificate from your country of residence (apostilled)
Health insurance valid in Portugal until you enter the public system
Employment contract, freelance client contracts, or company ownership documents proving the remote work
steps: Get your NIF (tax number) and open or prepare a Portuguese bank account — both can be arranged remotely
Gather documents: income proof for recent months, contracts, accommodation, criminal record (apostilled), insurance
Submit the D8 application at the Portuguese consulate (often via VFS Global) in your country of residence
Receive the four-month, double-entry visa and travel to Portugal
Attend your AIMA appointment in Portugal to convert the visa into a two-year residence permit (renewable for three more)

faqs.question: Can I bring my family on the Portugal D8 visa?
faqs.answer: Yes. Spouses, dependent children, and in some cases dependent parents can apply through family reunification, either together with your application or after you receive your residence permit. Each family member adds to the income requirement — roughly 50% more for a spouse and 30% per child.

faqs.question: Will I pay taxes in Portugal on the D8?
faqs.answer: Once you spend more than 183 days a year in Portugal you become a tax resident, taxed on worldwide income. The old NHR flat-rate regime closed to new applicants; a narrower incentive (IFICI/'NHR 2.0') exists for some professions. Get advice from a Portuguese tax professional before you commit — this is the part that surprises people.

faqs.question: Does freelance income count, or only employment?
faqs.answer: Both work. Employees show an employment contract and payslips; freelancers and business owners show client contracts, invoices, and bank statements. What matters is that the income is stable, documented, and comes from outside Portugal.

faqs.question: Is the D8 a path to EU citizenship?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the timeline doubled in 2026 and most guides still quote the old one. The D8 leads to a renewable residence permit and permanent residency after five years — that part is unchanged. Citizenship is the part that moved: Lei Orgânica n.º 1/2026, in force 19 May 2026, raised the naturalisation requirement from five years of legal residence to ten (seven for EU and CPLP nationals), alongside a basic language test. So an EU passport via the D8 is now a ten-year path for most applicants, not a five-year one.

records.renewal_note: The D8 residence permit runs two years, then renews for three — but you must actually be in Portugal for at least 16 months of that first two-year period. Note the 2026 change most guides still get wrong: Lei Orgânica n.º 1/2026, in force 19 May 2026, raised the residence required for naturalisation from six years to ten for most applicants, and from five to seven for EU and CPLP nationals. It also changed how the time is counted — legal residence now runs from the issue date of your residence card, so the wait for the card no longer counts toward the total. Applications already pending on 19 May 2026 keep the old rules. Permanent residency is unaffected and still available at five years.
records.tax_note: Ignore any guide still selling you NHR: the Non-Habitual Resident regime closed to new entrants in 2024 and was replaced by IFICI (often marketed as 'NHR 2.0'), which is much narrower. IFICI gives a flat 20% on qualifying income for ten years, but eligibility is restricted to specific activities — scientific research, technology, qualified roles in strategic sectors, startup work. A remote worker serving foreign clients generally does not qualify simply by holding a D8. Assume ordinary Portuguese rates on worldwide income unless a tax adviser confirms you fit IFICI. Note also that the habitual-residence test can make you resident below 183 days.
records.family_note: The income bar scales sharply: +50% for a partner and +30% per child on top of the main applicant's €3,680/month. A couple with two children needs roughly €7,700/month — more than double the single figure, which is where a lot of family applications quietly fail.
records.logistics_note: Two stages: the D8 visa at a Portuguese consulate in your country of residence, then the residence permit with AIMA once you have arrived. Consulate appointment waits are the usual bottleneck rather than the paperwork itself.

records.summary: Qatar does not offer a digital nomad visa. Employment in Qatar runs on employer sponsorship, there's no freelance-visa scheme, and the remote-work visa that's been rumoured since the mid-2020s hasn't materialised — only a five-year residence permit for exceptional talent and entrepreneurs has been announced. What exists in practice: visa-free or visa-on-arrival entry for dozens of nationalities, extendable in some cases, which is how the few nomads basing in Doha actually do it.
requirements: Status check (verified July 2026): no digital nomad or freelance visa exists — all in-country employment requires employer sponsorship
What you need today: a passport eligible for Qatar's visa-free or visa-on-arrival entry (dozens of nationalities qualify, typically for 30–90 days depending on passport)
Onward or return ticket and confirmed accommodation are commonly checked at entry
Remote work for foreign employers during a visit is tolerated in practice, but visitor status grants no right to work in the Qatari market
steps: Check your passport's entry allowance — many nationalities get visa-free entry or visa on arrival for 30 days (some up to 90), extendable in certain cases
For a short remote-work stint, enter as a visitor and keep your work strictly remote and foreign-paid; Doha's infrastructure, from fibre to coworking, is excellent
Need to stay long-term? The real routes are employer sponsorship, business setup in a Qatari free zone, or the announced five-year talent/entrepreneur residence permit
Watch official channels (Hukoomi, MOI) for a nomad-visa launch — it has been repeatedly rumoured but nothing has opened as of mid-2026

faqs.question: Does Qatar have a digital nomad visa?
faqs.answer: No. As of mid-2026 Qatar offers no digital nomad or remote-work visa, and no freelance visa either — all employment in the country runs through employer sponsorship. A longer-term remote-work pathway has been talked about for years and a five-year residence permit for exceptional talent and entrepreneurs has been announced, but nothing a typical remote worker can apply for exists today.

faqs.question: Can I work remotely from Qatar as a visitor?
faqs.answer: In practice, for a short stay, yes — dozens of nationalities enter visa-free or with a visa on arrival, typically for 30 to 90 days depending on the passport. Answering to a foreign employer from your hotel or a Doha coworking space isn't what visitor rules were written for, but it isn't policed as local employment. What visitor status absolutely doesn't allow is working for Qatari companies or clients.

faqs.question: What are Qatar's alternatives for a longer stay?
faqs.answer: Three real routes: get sponsored by a Qatari employer (the standard path), set up a company in one of Qatar's free zones and sponsor yourself through it, or qualify for the announced five-year residence permit aimed at exceptional talent and entrepreneurs. All are heavier lifts than a nomad visa — Qatar is currently a fine short-stint base but a poor fit for the classic nomad-visa play.

faqs.question: Which Middle East countries do offer nomad visas?
faqs.answer: The UAE is the regional standard-bearer — its virtual work residence visa gives remote workers a 12-month renewable stay with a clear application process, and Dubai has built a genuine nomad scene around it. If a Gulf base is the goal and Qatar's lack of a program rules it out, the UAE page on this site covers the requirements and application in full.

records.summary: Romania pairs a low cost of living with some of Europe's fastest internet, the medieval charm of Transylvania, and a lively hub in Bucharest — plus Schengen-area access. The catch is a steep income bar, pegged at roughly 3× the national average salary (around €5,000+/month). For higher earners wanting an affordable Eastern-European base, it delivers.
requirements: Monthly income of at least roughly 3× Romania's average gross salary (about RON 26,730 / €5,370+ per month), shown for the prior six months
Remote work for a company registered outside Romania, or your own foreign-registered business
Valid passport
Health insurance valid in Romania
Proof of accommodation in Romania
Clean criminal record
steps: Confirm your income meets the ~3× average-salary threshold (around €5,000+/month) over the last six months
Gather documents: passport, six months of income proof, employment/business proof, insurance, accommodation, criminal record
Apply online via Romania's Ministry of Foreign Affairs e-visa portal, or at a consulate, 2 weeks to 3 months before travel
Pay the €120 application fee; online decisions typically take 7–14 business days
Enter on the long-stay visa and obtain a residence permit; renewable, up to 3 years total on temporary residence

faqs.question: Why is Romania's income requirement so high?
faqs.answer: It's pegged at three times Romania's average gross monthly salary — roughly €5,000+/month, among the higher thresholds in Europe despite the country's low cost of living. You show it over the six months before applying.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: The visa leads to a residence permit that's renewable as long as you keep qualifying, up to a maximum of three years on temporary residence.

faqs.question: Does the visa include Schengen travel?
faqs.answer: Yes — Romania is in the Schengen area, so the visa comes with Schengen travel access alongside your stay in Romania.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Romania?
faqs.answer: If you become a tax resident (generally past 183 days) you may owe Romanian tax. Treatment of foreign income varies — confirm your situation with a local accountant before a long stay.

records.renewal_note: One year, renewable once — 24 months and the nomad route is exhausted, so staying longer means switching to a different permit. Whether the nomad time counts toward the five years for permanent residency is genuinely unsettled: reputable 2026 sources contradict each other, and we would rather say so than pick one. Confirm with the Romanian Immigration Office before planning around it. Separately, the long-stay visa fee rose from €120 to €300 on 27 April 2026.
records.tax_note: One of the strongest deals in Europe and not widely known: Law No. 69/2023 exempts digital nomad visa holders from Romanian income tax and social contributions on foreign-earned income. It pairs oddly with the visa's own 24-month ceiling — the tax treatment is excellent, the runway is short. Standard residency rules (183 days) still frame everything, and your home country taxes you on its own terms regardless.

records.summary: Serbia has no branded digital nomad visa — and doesn't need one. Most nationalities get 90 days visa-free, and the real long-stay route is a temporary residence permit based on remote work for foreign clients or on registering as an entrepreneur (the popular flat-tax 'pausalac' setup). Permits can now be issued for up to three years, Belgrade and Novi Sad have genuine nomad scenes, and the cost of living stays well below Western Europe.
requirements: Valid passport and legal entry to Serbia (most Western nationalities enter visa-free for 90 days)
Proof of remote income — authorities have applied a threshold of roughly €3,500/month over the preceding six months for the remote-worker route
Alternatively, registration as a Serbian entrepreneur (preduzetnik) — the flat-tax pausalac regime is the route most settling nomads actually use, with a much lower income bar
Registered address in Serbia (rental contract, and the white-card address registration done on arrival)
Health insurance valid in Serbia for the permit period
Clean criminal record certificate may be requested, depending on the basis of application
steps: Enter Serbia (visa-free for most passports) and complete the white-card address registration within 24 hours of arrival
Pick your basis: remote worker with foreign income, or register as a pausalac entrepreneur if you plan to settle — a local accountant makes this painless
Gather documents: income proof or business registration, lease, insurance, passport copies
Apply for the temporary residence permit online via the Welcome to Serbia portal (welcome.mup.gov.rs) or at the local MUP foreigners' office
Receive the permit — now issuable for up to three years — and renew before expiry; long-term residence becomes possible after several years

faqs.question: Does Serbia have a digital nomad visa?
faqs.answer: Not a branded one. Serbia created the practical equivalent instead: temporary residence permits granted on the basis of remote work for foreign employers or self-employment, now issuable for up to three years. Combined with 90 days visa-free entry for most passports, nomads test the city first and file for residence only if they want to stay.

faqs.question: How much income do I need for Serbian residence?
faqs.answer: For the remote-worker basis, authorities have applied a threshold of roughly €3,500 per month demonstrated over the preceding six months. The entrepreneur (pausalac) route has a far lower effective bar — you register a one-person business and pay a fixed monthly flat tax set by the municipality and activity code, which is why most nomads who settle in Serbia use it. Confirm current figures with MUP or a local advisor before filing.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Serbia?
faqs.answer: If you register as a pausalac entrepreneur, yes — a fixed monthly amount set by the tax administration regardless of actual earnings, which for many freelancers works out lower than Western European rates. Spending more than 183 days a year in Serbia generally makes you tax resident on worldwide income. Serbia has a wide treaty network; get local tax advice before committing.

faqs.question: Is Belgrade good for digital nomads?
faqs.answer: Genuinely, yes — fast internet, a lively cafe and coworking scene, Western-European-adjacent time zone, and living costs well below the EU capitals. Novi Sad is the calmer second option. The trade-offs: Serbia is outside the EU and Schengen (no visa-free onward EU residence), and English is less universal in official settings — one more reason locals recommend an accountant for the paperwork.

records.renewal_note: Renewable for up to three years at a time, and the timelines are unusually short — permanent residence after three years of temporary residence, with naturalisation possible on the same three-year clock and no language exam, just a written declaration that you consider Serbia home. The catch is severe: Serbia generally requires you to renounce your existing citizenship to naturalise. Renew no earlier than three months and no later than one month before expiry.
records.tax_note: We could not find a published nomad-specific tax exemption here, and we are not going to assume one exists — nor assume it doesn't. What is solid: residents are taxed on worldwide income, and passing 183 days in a year normally makes you resident. Confirm the current position with the national tax authority before you plan around it.

records.summary: Seychelles is a bucket-list Indian Ocean archipelago — granite peaks, white-sand beaches, and turquoise water — that opened its Workcation program to remote workers. There's no fixed income minimum (just proof you can support yourself), the fee is a flat €45, foreign income isn't taxed locally, and you can stay up to a year. The catch is cost of living: paradise here isn't cheap.
requirements: Proof of sufficient funds to support your stay (no fixed income minimum) — typically 3–6 months of bank statements
Remote work as a freelancer, business owner, or employee for entities outside Seychelles
Valid passport
Valid medical and travel insurance
Proof of employment or business ownership
steps: Gather documents: passport, bank statements, proof of remote work, medical/travel insurance
Apply for the Visitors Workcation Permit (VWP) at the official portal (seychelles.govtas.com), at least 60 days before arrival
Pay the one-time €45 fee
Once the VWP is validated, complete the Health Travel Authorization (HTA) for entry
Receive approval (usually 5–10 business days) and travel; the permit allows stays up to one year

faqs.question: Is there an income requirement?
faqs.answer: No fixed minimum. Instead of a salary threshold, you show proof of sufficient funds to support yourself — usually via bank statements. You must work for foreign entities, not take up local employment.

faqs.question: Will I be taxed in Seychelles?
faqs.answer: No local tax on foreign-sourced income — a standout benefit of the Workcation program. You may still have home-country obligations depending on your citizenship.

faqs.question: How much does it cost?
faqs.answer: A flat one-time fee of €45 for the Workcation Permit application — cheap, though the islands' cost of living is high once you're there.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: From 30 days up to one year. You must apply for the permit at least 60 days before you plan to arrive.

records.renewal_note: Up to 12 months, with extensions possible while you still meet the conditions. Seychelles permanent residency is its own route requiring five or more years of continuous legal residence, and nothing published ties the Workcation Retreat to it — assume it doesn't count unless Immigration tells you otherwise.
records.tax_note: Workcation Retreat holders are not subject to Seychelles tax on income earned from outside the country — the exemption is one of the programme's main selling points. As always it exempts you locally and does nothing about your home country's claim on the same income.

records.summary: South Africa offers world-class scenery, Cape Town's strong nomad scene, and a Western lifestyle at a low cost of living, with the rand stretching foreign income far. The Remote Work Visa, introduced in 2024, lets you live here for up to three years on income earned abroad. The income bar is high and processing can be slow, but for a long, affordable base in an English-speaking country it's hard to beat.
requirements: Foreign income of at least ZAR 650,976/year (about $3,000/month), from employers or clients outside South Africa
A genuine remote-work arrangement — employed or contracted to a foreign company, with no South African employer
Valid passport and two passport photos
Proof of accommodation in South Africa
Police clearance from every country lived in for 12+ months in the last five years
Bank statements (3–6 months), employment or freelance contracts, and tax returns
steps: Confirm your foreign income meets the ZAR 650,976/year threshold
Gather documents: passport, bank statements, contracts, tax returns, accommodation proof, police clearance
Apply at a South African mission abroad or via the Department of Home Affairs eVisa/ePermit system
Wait out processing — typically 4–8 weeks depending on the mission
Receive the visa (issued from over 3 months up to 3 years); renew if you stay long-term

faqs.question: Can I work for a South African company on this visa?
faqs.answer: No. The Remote Work Visa is strictly for income from foreign employers or clients — you're not entitled to take up local employment in South Africa under it.

faqs.question: Will I pay South African tax?
faqs.answer: If you stay more than 183 days in a 12-month period you generally become a tax resident and must register with SARS. A double-taxation agreement between South Africa and your home country can reduce or remove double tax — check whether yours applies.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: The visa can be issued for more than three months and up to three years, and renewed, for a stay of up to three years total — one of the longer nomad visas available.

faqs.question: Is the income requirement really that high?
faqs.answer: Yes — ZAR 650,976/year, though this was reduced from ZAR 1,000,000 in late 2024. It must be foreign income, shown via bank statements, contracts, and tax returns.

records.renewal_note: One year initially, renewable to three years total. It is a visitor's visa with a remote-work endorsement, so it does not build toward permanent residence — that route runs through a Critical Skills or General Work visa followed by five years on it. Time on the remote-work visa doesn't carry over, so switching earlier rather than later matters if you intend to stay.
records.tax_note: Treat this one carefully — South African advisers openly call it a tax trap for the unwary. There is NO blanket exemption for remote-work visa holders: tax residency is decided by South African law, not by which visa you hold, so a long stay can make you resident and bring worldwide income into scope. One narrow relief exists: where the visa is issued for six months or less within a 36-month window, you may apply to SARS for exemption. The R1.25 million foreign employment income exemption is a different thing — it is relief for South African residents working abroad, not for foreigners working here.

records.summary: South Korea's F-1-D 'workation' visa opens Seoul's hyper-connected, dynamic city life — the world's best mobile internet, safety, and food — to remote workers. The income bar is steep (about $66,000/year, twice Korea's GNI per capita) and it requires real insurance and work history, but for fans of Korea wanting up to two years, it's the legitimate route.
requirements: Annual income of at least about ₩88.1 million (~$66,000) — roughly twice Korea's GNI per capita
At least one year of work experience in the same industry
Remote work for a foreign employer or your own overseas business; no Korean clients or employers
Private medical insurance with coverage of at least ₩100 million (~$75,000)
Clean criminal record (FBI check apostilled for US applicants)
Valid passport
steps: Confirm your income meets the ~$66,000/year bar and you have a year of relevant work experience
Gather documents: passport, income proof, employment proof, apostilled criminal background check, insurance
Apply at a Korean consulate or embassy in your home country
Wait out processing — typically 3–4 weeks
Receive the F-1-D visa, valid one year and renewable once for two years total

faqs.question: How much income do I need?
faqs.answer: About ₩88.1 million/year (~$66,000), roughly twice Korea's GNI per capita — one of the highest nomad-visa thresholds in the world.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: One year on first issue, renewable once, for a maximum of two years.

faqs.question: Can I work for Korean companies?
faqs.answer: No. The visa is strictly for remote work serving foreign employers or clients; you can't take up local Korean employment.

faqs.question: What insurance do I need?
faqs.answer: Private medical insurance covering at least ₩100 million (~$75,000) for hospital treatment and medical repatriation — Korea requires substantial coverage.

records.renewal_note: Renewed annually up to three years total. Worth knowing how new this is: the F-1-D left pilot status and launched properly on 30 June 2026, which both raised the ceiling from two years to three and lowered the income thresholds (now scaled to age and region, roughly one to two times per-capita GNI). Anything written before mid-2026 describes the pilot. F-1 is not a settlement category, so treat permanent residency as a separate track and confirm current rules with Korea Immigration.
records.tax_note: Korea uses the 183-day test, and here the visa and the threshold pull in opposite directions: use the F-1-D for its full year and you will cross 183 days and become a Korean tax resident. The saving grace is structural — the F-1-D forbids working for Korean companies, so your remote income is foreign-sourced and Korea does not tax it. Under 183 days you are plainly outside the system.

records.summary: Spain's digital nomad visa, created by the 2023 Startup Law, is one of Europe's most generous: apply from inside Spain as a tourist and receive a three-year residence permit directly, with an optional flat-tax regime for new residents. Big-city energy in Madrid and Barcelona, islands and coast everywhere else, and full Schengen access included.
requirements: Remote income of at least 200% of the Spanish minimum wage (SMI) per month — higher with family members
Work for companies outside Spain — Spanish clients may account for at most 20% of your income
Your employer or main client relationship must be at least three months old, and the company operating for at least one year
A university degree or at least three years of relevant professional experience
Social security coverage: a certificate of coverage from your home country, or registering as self-employed (autónomo) in Spain
Clean criminal record certificate (apostilled) and full private health insurance, or public enrollment via autónomo
steps: Gather documents — income proof, contracts, degree or experience evidence, criminal record with apostille, insurance — with sworn Spanish translations where required
Choose your route: apply at a Spanish consulate abroad (one-year visa), or enter Spain and apply to the UGE online for the three-year residence permit directly
Get your NIE (foreigner ID number) — assigned during the process if you don't have one
Wait for the UGE decision — the law sets short response windows, and silence counts as approval in many cases
Once approved, book the fingerprint appointment and collect your TIE residence card

faqs.question: What is the Beckham Law and can nomads use it?
faqs.answer: Spain's special expat regime (the 'Beckham Law') lets qualifying new residents pay a flat 24% tax on Spanish-source employment income up to €600,000 for up to six years, instead of progressive rates. Employees on the nomad visa can often opt in; self-employed applicants usually can't. Apply within six months of registering — and confirm specifics with a Spanish tax advisor.

faqs.question: Can I apply for Spain's nomad visa while already in Spain?
faqs.answer: Yes — that's the unusual part. You can enter as a tourist and apply online to the UGE (Unidad de Grandes Empresas) from inside Spain, receiving the full three-year residence permit directly rather than the one-year consulate visa.

faqs.question: How much Spanish client work is allowed?
faqs.answer: Up to 20% of your total income can come from Spanish companies. The core of your work must be remote for employers or clients outside Spain — cross that line and you're in regular work-permit territory.

faqs.question: Does Spain's visa lead to permanent residency?
faqs.answer: Yes. The permit renews in two-year blocks, permanent residency is available after five years of continuous legal residence, and citizenship after ten (two years for citizens of Ibero-American countries). Time on the nomad visa counts.

records.renewal_note: The in-country permit runs three years and extends by two. Renewal expects you to genuinely live in Spain — at least 183 days a year — so it doesn't suit a rotating base. Citizenship normally takes ten years, but nationals of Ibero-American countries, Andorra, the Philippines, Equatorial Guinea and Portugal qualify after two.
records.tax_note: The Beckham Law caps tax at a flat 24% (on income up to €600,000) for six years instead of progressive rates reaching 47%, and DNV holders were explicitly made eligible by the Startups Act. The distinction that decides your bill: if you are EMPLOYED by a foreign company you can opt in — if you are a FREELANCER invoicing clients, you generally cannot, and you face progressive rates of 19–47% on worldwide income plus compulsory autónomos social security. Same visa, very different outcome. You also must not have been a Spanish tax resident in the previous five years.
records.logistics_note: Where you apply changes what you get, which is unusual and worth planning around: from a Spanish consulate abroad you receive a one-year visa, whereas applying from inside Spain as a legal visitor yields a three-year residence authorisation. Same programme, three times the runway.

records.summary: Sri Lanka launched its digital nomad visa in February 2026, opening the island's beaches, tea-country highlands, and wildlife to remote workers at a low cost of living. The bar is accessible — $2,000/month — and holders can open local bank accounts and enrol kids in school. A fresh, well-rounded base in South Asia for up to a year, renewable.
requirements: Monthly income of at least $2,000 (plus $500/month per dependent), earned entirely from outside Sri Lanka
Be 18 or older, working remotely for a foreign company, freelancing for international clients, or running a business not registered in Sri Lanka
International health insurance covering treatment in Sri Lanka for the whole stay
Valid passport
Proof of foreign income remittance
steps: Confirm your foreign income meets the $2,000/month threshold
Gather documents: passport, proof of foreign income, health insurance
Submit your application to the Department of Immigration & Emigration (Residence Visa Division) and pay the ~$500 fee
Wait for review and approval (typically about 2–4 weeks)
Receive the visa endorsed in your passport; valid up to 12 months, renewable annually

faqs.question: How much income do I need?
faqs.answer: At least $2,000/month, plus $500/month per dependent, all earned from foreign sources. You must show the income clearly originates outside Sri Lanka.

faqs.question: What can I do on the visa?
faqs.answer: Beyond living and working remotely, holders can open Sri Lankan bank accounts, enrol dependent children in private or international schools, and use coworking spaces and government tourism events.

faqs.question: How long can I stay?
faqs.answer: Up to 12 months initially, renewable annually as long as you keep meeting the requirements.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Sri Lanka?
faqs.answer: The visa is for foreign-source income and doesn't permit local earnings. Confirm your tax position with an adviser if you stay long-term.

records.renewal_note: 365 days, renewable annually — and the ceiling moved recently: 2026 updates extended the maximum from one year renewable once to as much as five years, alongside lower income thresholds. Renewals require the original document set again plus proof of tax registration with the Sri Lanka Inland Revenue Department, which is worth planning for. Sri Lanka has published nothing linking the visa to permanent residency, so treat settlement as a separate question.
records.tax_note: Foreign income is generally not taxed locally, but the visa explicitly does not exempt you from Sri Lankan tax and reporting obligations, and the position depends on your residency status. One practical requirement catches people: renewing beyond the initial year requires proof of tax registration with the Inland Revenue Department — mandatory even if every cent you earn comes from abroad. Register early rather than at renewal time.

records.summary: Taiwan offers world-class food, safety, fast internet, and an affordable, well-connected base in Taipei. Its dedicated digital nomad visa — expanded in January 2026 from six months to a full two years — is a clean, purpose-built route for remote workers, with income tiers by age and a savings requirement. High earners can alternatively use the Employment Gold Card.
records.income_original: $20,000 per year in your twenties, $40,000 per year from age 30
requirements: For applicants 30+, annual income of at least $40,000 in one of the last two years; for ages 20–29, at least $20,000
Alternatively, proof you already hold a digital nomad visa from another country
Bank deposits averaging at least $10,000/month over the last six months
Remote work via digital means, with no services provided to Taiwan-based businesses or employers
International medical and hospitalization insurance covering your stay (nomads can't join Taiwan's NHI)
Eligibility for visa-exempt entry to Taiwan
steps: Confirm your income (≥$40,000/yr if 30+, ≥$20,000 if 20–29) and ~$10,000/month average savings
Gather documents: passport, income proof, six months of bank statements, insurance
Apply at a Taiwan overseas mission, which forwards your case to the National Development Council (NDC); or, if already in Taiwan visa-exempt, apply to BOCA before your stay expires
Receive the multiple-entry digital nomad visa
Enter on a 6-month stay, extendable three times (6 months each) up to two years total

faqs.question: How long can I stay in Taiwan?
faqs.answer: Up to two years. Taiwan expanded the visa in January 2026 from a single six-month stay to a 6-month initial period plus three 6-month extensions — a maximum of two years.

faqs.question: What are the income requirements?
faqs.answer: $40,000/year if you're 30 or older, or $20,000/year if you're 20–29 (in one of the last two years), plus average bank deposits of about $10,000/month over six months.

faqs.question: Gold Card or Digital Nomad Visa?
faqs.answer: The dedicated Digital Nomad Visa is purpose-built for remote workers. High earners and certain professionals may instead qualify for the Taiwan Employment Gold Card, which grants residency and open work rights for up to three years.

faqs.question: Can I use Taiwan's health system?
faqs.answer: Not on this visa — digital nomad visa holders can't enroll in National Health Insurance, so you must carry private international medical insurance for your whole stay.

records.renewal_note: Six months initially, extendable through successive renewals to a maximum of two years. This programme is brand new — Taiwan's National Development Council only formalised it in July 2026 — so expect procedural detail to move and verify against the NDC before committing. Income thresholds are age-scaled: roughly $20,000 a year in your twenties, $40,000 from thirty.
records.tax_note: Past 183 days you may be deemed tax resident, bringing worldwide income into scope at progressive rates. Taiwan does offer a first-time foreign professional incentive — a 50% exemption on salary above roughly US$102,000 for up to five years — but note the shape of it: it only helps above a high threshold, so it does nothing for most nomads. Taiwan extended the visa itself from six months to two years in January 2026, which makes crossing the residency line far more likely than it used to be.

records.summary: Thailand's DTV changed the game for Asia-based nomads: a five-year, multiple-entry visa with 180 days per stay, no monthly income requirement — just a savings threshold — and a fee that undercuts almost every Western nomad visa. If your life runs through Bangkok, Chiang Mai, or the islands, this is the one to get.
requirements: Savings of at least 500,000 THB (roughly $14,000–15,000) held for the last three months, shown via bank statements
Proof of remote work for an employer or clients outside Thailand (the 'workcation' track), or enrollment in a Thai soft-power activity (Muay Thai, cooking school, medical treatment)
Passport valid for at least six months at application
Application submitted from outside Thailand via the official e-visa portal
Working for Thai employers or serving Thai customers is not permitted on this visa
steps: Prepare documents: three months of bank statements showing the 500k THB balance, employment or client contracts, passport scan, photo
Apply online at the official Thai e-visa portal from your country of residence or any country where you hold residency
Pay the 10,000 THB fee and wait for the embassy's review (typically days to a few weeks)
Receive the e-visa by email and enter Thailand — each entry grants 180 days
Extend once per entry for another 180 days at immigration, or reset with a border run; repeat for five years

faqs.question: How does the 180-day stay actually work on the DTV?
faqs.answer: Each time you enter Thailand you get 180 days. You can extend that once at a local immigration office for roughly another 180 days (extension fee applies), or leave and re-enter for a fresh 180. The visa itself stays valid for five years of unlimited entries.

faqs.question: Do I become a Thai tax resident on the DTV?
faqs.answer: If you spend 180 days or more in Thailand in a calendar year, yes — and Thailand has been tightening rules on taxing foreign income remitted into the country. If you plan near-full-time Thailand living, talk to a tax advisor about what you remit and when.

faqs.question: Can my spouse and kids come too?
faqs.answer: Yes. Spouses and dependent children under 20 can apply for DTVs as dependents, with their own applications and the same fee. The 500k THB financial proof generally needs to cover the family.

faqs.question: Can I work for a Thai company on the DTV?
faqs.answer: No. The DTV covers remote work for foreign employers and clients only. Working for Thai businesses or serving Thai customers requires a proper work permit under a different visa category.

records.renewal_note: The DTV is a five-year multiple-entry visa, which is not the same as five years of residence. Each entry grants 180 days, extendable once by another 180 at an immigration office, so 360 consecutive days is the practical maximum before you must leave and re-enter — and entries are unlimited across the five years. On permanent residency, be careful with confident answers either way: Thai PR requires three consecutive years holding a Non-Immigrant visa, and the LTR visa is explicitly excluded. The DTV is its own category rather than a Non-Immigrant extension, so it is very unlikely to qualify — but Thai Immigration has published nothing specific about the DTV, so we're flagging the mechanism rather than asserting a rule.
records.tax_note: Note the threshold: Thailand uses 180 days in a calendar year, not the 183 most countries use, and people miscount it. Cross it and you are a Thai tax resident — at which point foreign income earned from 1 January 2024 onward is taxable when you REMIT it into Thailand. The old 'bring it in the following year and it's untaxed' route was closed in 2024. Stay under 180 days and foreign income is outside the net entirely, which is why the DTV's 180-day entries and the tax line sit so close together — that is not a coincidence, and it is worth planning around deliberately.
records.family_note: A spouse and unmarried children under 20 can be included as dependants, and they may also apply separately rather than only alongside you.
records.logistics_note: Note what Thailand actually tests: not a monthly income figure but ฿500,000 of accessible funds. Applied for at a Thai embassy or consulate; the 180-day extension per entry is then handled at an immigration office inside Thailand.

records.summary: Dubai's remote work visa is the zero-income-tax play: a one-year renewable residence for remote workers earning $3,500/month, with an Emirates ID, local banking, and the best flight connectivity on the planet. Summer is brutal; October to April is why people stay.
requirements: Proof of remote work for an employer or company outside the UAE (contract of 1+ year) or ownership of a foreign company
Monthly income of at least $3,500, with 3 months of bank statements and payslips
Passport valid 6+ months and health insurance valid in the UAE
Application online (federal portal) or through Dubai's virtual working programme
Renewable annually while you still meet the criteria
steps: Gather employment/company proof, income statements, insurance
Apply online via the UAE federal channels or Dubai's dedicated programme
Pay fees, complete medical testing and biometrics on arrival
Receive the residence visa and Emirates ID — unlocks local banking, leases, and schooling

faqs.question: Is the UAE really tax-free for nomads?
faqs.answer: There's no personal income tax on salaries or freelance income, including foreign remote income. The 9% corporate tax targets business profits, not employment income. Your home country's rules (especially for US citizens) still follow you.

faqs.question: Dubai is expensive — does $3,500/month actually work?
faqs.answer: That's the visa floor, not a comfortable Dubai budget. Realistic comfortable living starts around $4,500–5,500/month with rent. Sharjah, Ajman, or older Dubai neighborhoods stretch it further.

faqs.question: Does the remote work visa lead to long-term UAE residency?
faqs.answer: It renews annually but doesn't accrue toward permanent status. Long-term plays in the UAE run through Golden Visas (10-year, investment or talent-based) — some nomads graduate to those later.

records.renewal_note: One year, renewable annually by fresh application for as long as you keep meeting the income and insurance bar — there's no published ceiling on renewals. It is not a route to settlement: the UAE has no general permanent residency or naturalisation for expatriates, and long-term stay runs through separate schemes such as the Golden Visa. Practically, though, it behaves like residency: you get an Emirates ID, banking, telecoms and schooling without a local sponsor.
records.tax_note: The UAE levies no personal income tax on individuals — confirmed by the Federal Tax Authority and PwC's 2026 tax summaries. If you have seen a claim that the UAE introduced a 5% personal income tax on 1 January 2026, it is wrong: the 5% is VAT, in force since 2018, and at least one widely-shared article conflated the two. There is a 9% corporate tax on business profits above a threshold, which can matter if you invoice through a UAE company rather than being employed.
records.family_note: Virtual work visa holders can sponsor a spouse and children for the same duration as their own residency, which is confirmed by the GDRFA rather than inferred. Dependants need their own UAE-valid health insurance, and the $3,500/month income bar applies to you as sponsor.
records.logistics_note: Filed online through the Virtual Working Programme. You will need UAE-valid health insurance in place, and the income evidence is checked against bank statements rather than a contract alone.

records.summary: Uruguay is the quiet, stable choice in South America — safe, democratic, and relaxed, with beach towns like Punta del Este and a livable capital in Montevideo. The Digital Nomad Permit has no minimum income and costs almost nothing: you enter as a tourist, file a short online form with a sworn declaration of means, and you're set for six months. A territorial tax system means foreign income generally isn't taxed.
requirements: Self-employment or remote work for companies or clients outside Uruguay
A sworn declaration confirming you have sufficient means to support yourself (no fixed income minimum; nomads typically show $1,500–$2,000/month)
Valid passport (most nationalities enter visa-free as tourists to begin the process)
Be physically in Uruguay to apply
For renewal: a clean criminal record from each country you've legally resided in for 6+ months over the last five years, plus a vaccination certificate issued in Uruguay
steps: Enter Uruguay as a regular tourist — most nationalities can do this visa-free
Go to the national migration portal and select 'Residencia Provisoria – Nómadas Digitales'
Fill out the short online form and upload your passport plus a sworn declaration of financial means
Pay the small administrative fee (around $10–$15) when prompted later in the process
Receive a six-month permit, renewable once for another six months — or convert to temporary/permanent residency if you decide to stay

faqs.question: Is there an income requirement for Uruguay's nomad permit?
faqs.answer: No fixed minimum. Instead of a salary threshold, you sign a sworn declaration that you can financially support yourself during your stay. Most nomads demonstrate around $1,500–$2,000/month in practice, but Uruguay doesn't set a hard number.

faqs.question: Do I have to be in Uruguay to apply?
faqs.answer: Yes. You enter as a tourist first — most nationalities can do this visa-free — and then start the digital nomad permit application online from inside the country through the National Migration Office.

faqs.question: How does Uruguay tax my income?
faqs.answer: Uruguay uses a territorial tax system, so income earned from foreign employers or clients is generally not subject to Uruguayan income tax. There are also multi-year tax incentives for new residents — worth confirming with a local accountant if you settle long-term.

faqs.question: Can the permit lead to longer-term residency?
faqs.answer: Yes. The permit runs six months and is renewable once for another six. If you decide to stay, Uruguay offers a relatively accessible path to temporary and then permanent legal residency, which many nomads transition into.

records.renewal_note: 180 days, extendable once by another 180 — twelve months and it expires. The extension needs a criminal record certificate. The permit itself establishes no residency and none of the time counts toward it, but Uruguay is unusual in that the separate legal-residency route is genuinely accessible, and citizenship from there is among the more attainable in the region. Treat the nomad permit as a look-around, then switch deliberately.
records.tax_note: Uruguay taxes territorially: foreign-earned income is not taxed here, and that has held despite OECD pressure to move to worldwide taxation. New tax residents also get an 11-year holiday on foreign dividends and interest, after which those are taxed at a flat 12% — note that is passive income, not your remote salary, which is a distinction several guides get wrong. Holding the nomad permit does not by itself make you tax resident, but passing 183 days in a calendar year can. The DGI has been scrutinising foreign-source claims harder lately, so keep contracts, client records and bank statements.

records.summary: Vietnam has no digital nomad visa and no retirement visa, and as of 2026 neither is close to existing — a ten-year 'golden visa' was proposed in April 2025 and has not been enacted. That matters because a lot of people are looking for one: searches for a Vietnamese retirement visa run into the hundreds every month and every result is either an agency selling something else or a guide describing a visa that was never created. What people actually do is live here on repeated 90-day e-visas, which is legal and cheap and is not residence — you accrue no status, no path to permanence, and no protection if the rules change. Anyone offering you a Vietnamese retirement visa is selling you a different product under that name.
requirements: Status check (verified August 2026): Vietnam operates no digital nomad visa and no retirement visa. There is no application to make and no income threshold to meet, because neither category exists
What does exist: a 90-day e-visa, single or multiple entry, applied for online at the government portal — roughly USD 25 single-entry and USD 50 multiple-entry
Passport valid at least six months beyond entry, a passport photo and a scan of the photo page

A Temporary Residence Card is the only route to actual residence, and it is granted on a separate basis — employment with a work permit, investment, or marriage to a Vietnamese citizen. Remote work for foreign clients is not one of the bases

Working remotely for foreign employers while on an e-visa sits in a grey area Vietnam has not formally addressed. It is widely done and not obviously permitted; we are not going to tell you it is fine when the government has not said so
steps: Apply for the 90-day e-visa at the official portal before travelling — it is the only route most remote workers will use, and it is issued in about 3–5 working days
Choose multiple entry if you intend to leave and return; single entry ends the moment you cross the border out
Plan for the reset: at 90 days you leave and re-enter on a fresh e-visa. Budget the flights and accept that entry is always at an officer's discretion

If you want real residence rather than repeated visits, work backwards from the Temporary Residence Card bases — a work permit through a Vietnamese employer, an investment, or marriage. There is no remote-work route to a TRC
Track your days. Tax residency starts at 183 days in a 12-month period, and repeated e-visas make it easy to cross without noticing

faqs.question: Does Vietnam have a retirement visa?
faqs.answer: No. Vietnam has never operated a retirement visa, and there is no announced plan to create one. If a site is walking you through 'Vietnam retirement visa requirements', it is describing something that does not exist — usually to sell you an agency service for a 90-day e-visa or a Temporary Residence Card you probably don't qualify for. Retirees who live in Vietnam do it on repeated e-visas, or on a TRC obtained through marriage or investment.

faqs.question: Is there a Vietnam digital nomad visa?
faqs.answer: No. Unlike Thailand, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Malaysia, Vietnam has no visa category built for remote workers. A ten-year golden visa was proposed in April 2025; as of 2026 it has not been enacted, and a proposal is not a visa. The practical route is the 90-day e-visa, repeated.

faqs.question: Can I just keep renewing the 90-day e-visa?
faqs.answer: In practice many people do, by leaving and re-entering. Understand what you are choosing: each entry is discretionary, you accumulate no residence status, there is no path to permanence, and a rule change can end the arrangement with no notice and no grandfathering. It is a way to be in Vietnam. It is not a way to move to Vietnam.

faqs.question: Will I pay tax in Vietnam?
faqs.answer: If you are present 183 days or more in a 12-month period you are generally a Vietnamese tax resident, and residents are taxed on worldwide income at progressive rates. Repeated 90-day entries make it easy to cross that line without noticing. Your home country may tax you regardless — US citizens are taxed on worldwide income wherever they live. Take advice against your own treaty position before you cross 183 days, not after.

faqs.question: Where should I look instead?
faqs.answer: If a formal long-stay route is what you need, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Sri Lanka all operate one, and we hold verified records for each. Thailand in particular has both a five-year remote-work visa and a one-year retirement route, so it answers both of the questions Vietnam cannot.

records.renewal_note: There is nothing to renew, because there is no long-stay permission to hold. The 90-day e-visa is not extended from inside the country in the ordinary case — you leave and apply again. Time spent on repeated e-visas counts toward nothing: not residence, not permanent residence, not naturalisation. That is the honest difference between Vietnam and every other country in this dataset with an open route.
records.tax_note: 183 days in a 12-month period, and note that it is a rolling 12 months rather than a calendar year — which is stricter than Thailand's 180-day calendar-year test and catches people who assume the clock resets in January. Vietnamese tax residents are taxable on worldwide income at progressive rates. The trap specific to this country is structural: the only realistic way to stay long-term is repeated 90-day entries, and repeated 90-day entries are an efficient way to accumulate 183 days without ever making a decision about it.
records.family_note: Not applicable in the usual sense — there is no long-stay visa to add dependants to. Each person travels on their own e-visa. Marriage to a Vietnamese citizen is one of the bases for a Temporary Residence Card, which is a different application with its own conditions.
records.logistics_note: The e-visa is applied for online at the government portal and issued in about 3–5 working days; roughly USD 25 single-entry, USD 50 multiple-entry. Use the official site — this is one of the most impersonated visa applications in the region, and the agency copies charge several times the government fee for the same form.
